choices.why: Correct — negative × negative = positive. Then round 6.406061 to 2 d.p. → 6.41.

choices.label: Negative — because the base is negative
choices.why: Squaring removes the sign. (−a)² = a². The result is always ≥ 0.

choices.label: Same as −(2.531²) = −6.406
choices.why: −2.531² would negate after squaring. But (−2.531)² squares the whole negative number → positive.

61.prompt: From a graph showing a line falling left to right through (0, 3), which equation applies?

choices.label: y = −2x + 3 — negative slope (falls left to right), y-intercept +3
choices.why: Correct — falling line → negative m. Crosses y-axis at 3 → c = +3. Equation: y = −2x + 3.

choices.label: y = 2x + 3 — positive slope, same y-intercept
choices.why: Positive slope means the line rises from left to right. This line falls — slope must be negative.

choices.label: y = −2x − 3 — negative slope but negative y-intercept
choices.why: The graph passes through (0, 3), so c = +3, not −3.

65.prompt: In a right triangle with hypotenuse 20 and angle 40°, which expression gives the opposite side?

choices.label: opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ = 20 sin 40°  (SOH: sin = opposite/hypotenuse)
choices.why: Correct — SOH: sin 40° = opposite/20. Rearrange: opposite = 20 × sin 40°.

choices.label: opposite = hypotenuse × cos θ = 20 cos 40°  (CAH: cos = adjacent/hypotenuse)
choices.why: Cosine uses the side adjacent to the angle, not opposite. Use sine for the opposite side.

choices.label: opposite = hypotenuse × tan θ = 20 tan 40°  (TOA: tan = opposite/adjacent)
choices.why: Tangent uses opposite/adjacent — not the hypotenuse. When hypotenuse is involved, use sin or cos.

66.prompt: A price of $180 increases by 2.5% annually for 3 years. Which formula gives the new price?

choices.label: New price = 180 × (1.025)³ — compound growth at 2.5% per year
choices.why: Correct — the factor (1+r) = 1.025 is applied 3 times. This is the same structure as compound interest.

choices.label: New price = 180 + 180 × 0.025 × 3 = 180 + 13.50 — simple annual increase
choices.why: That's simple (linear) growth — same dollar amount each year. Compound growth re-applies the % to the growing base.

choices.label: New price = 180 × (1 + 0.025 × 3) = 180 × 1.075
choices.why: Adding total rate×time is simple growth. Compound uses exponentiation: (1.025)³ ≠ 1.075.

67.prompt: A bill has parts GST-included and parts GST-excluded. How is total GST calculated?

choices.label: GST from included part: total÷1.1 then subtract. GST from excluded: ×0.10. Add both amounts.
choices.why: Correct — each component handled separately. GST-included: extract via /1.1. GST-excluded: add 10%. Sum them.

choices.label: Apply 10% to the combined total of both components
choices.why: The included component already has GST — applying 10% again would double-count.

choices.label: Only the excluded component has GST; the included part doesn't
choices.why: The included part still has GST — you just extract it differently (price/1.1 to find base, then subtract).

68.prompt: 6 painters take 20 days. Using inverse variation, how long for 15 painters?

choices.label: T₁×N₁ = T₂×N₂. So 6×20 = 15×T₂. T₂ = 120÷15 = 8 days.
choices.why: Correct — total painter-days (work) stays constant. More painters → fewer days proportionally.

choices.label: T₂ = T₁ × (N₂/N₁) = 20 × (15/6) = 50 days — more painters, more days
choices.why: More painters reduce time, not increase it. Inverse: multiply by the RECIPROCAL ratio: T₂ = 20 × (6/15) = 8.

choices.label: T₂ = T₁ − (N₂ − N₁) = 20 − 9 = 11 days — subtract extra painters
choices.why: Inverse variation is multiplicative (constant product), not additive (constant difference).

69.prompt: To make p the subject of s = wt + p/2, which sequence of steps is correct?

choices.label: 1. Subtract wt from both sides → s−wt = p/2  2. Multiply both sides by 2 → p = 2s − 2wt
choices.why: Correct — reverse BODMAS: undo addition of wt (subtract), then undo division by 2 (multiply). Result: p = 2(s−wt).

choices.label: 1. Multiply both sides by 2 first → 2s = 2wt + p  2. Subtract 2wt → p = 2s − 2wt
choices.why: Also correct — multiplying by 2 first distributes across both terms on the right. Same answer either way.

choices.label: Divide both sides by 2 to isolate p: p = s/2 − wt
choices.why: Dividing s by 2 makes p/4 (not p). You need to MULTIPLY by 2 (not divide) to clear the denominator.

70.prompt: Train departs 6:42am, arrives 8:04am, travels 61km. What's the average speed?

choices.label: Step 1: Time = 82 minutes = 82/60 hours. Step 2: Speed = 61 ÷ (82/60) ≈ 45 km/h.
choices.why: Correct — convert time to hours first. 6:42 to 8:04 = 82 minutes. Speed = distance ÷ time in hours.

choices.label: Speed = 61 ÷ 2 = 30.5 km/h — just use the hour difference
choices.why: The journey is 1 hour 22 minutes (82 min), not 2 hours. Always convert to decimal hours accurately.

choices.label: Speed = 61 × 60 ÷ 82 — multiply distance by 60
choices.why: Also correct — this converts km/min to km/h: (61/82) km/min × 60 min/h ≈ 44.6 km/h ≈ 45 km/h.

71.prompt: To find the % of over-30s (157 total) who watch Anime (34 do), which calculation applies?

choices.label: % = (34 ÷ 157) × 100 ≈ 22% — part of subgroup ÷ total in subgroup
choices.why: Correct — use the subgroup totals only (157 over-30s). The overall 370 is irrelevant here.

choices.label: % = (34 ÷ 370) × 100 — divide by overall survey total
choices.why: This gives % of all respondents who are over-30 Anime watchers — not the % within the over-30 subgroup.

choices.label: % = (157 ÷ 34) × 100 — total over-30s ÷ Anime watchers
choices.why: Inverted — part goes in the numerator. % = part/whole × 100 = 34/157 × 100.

72.prompt: Loan $9000, repay $300/month for 4 years. Using I = Prt, what is the annual interest rate?

choices.label: Total repaid = 300×48 = $14,400. Interest I = 14,400−9,000 = $5,400. r = I÷(P×t) = 5400÷(9000×4) = 15%.
choices.why: Correct — rearrange I = Prt to find r. First calculate total interest paid, then divide by P×t.

choices.label: r = monthly payment ÷ principal = 300 ÷ 9000 ≈ 3.3% per month
choices.why: This gives a monthly rate that doesn't account for the loan term. Use total interest over total time.

choices.label: r = total repaid ÷ principal ÷ time = 14,400 ÷ 9,000 ÷ 4 = 0.4 = 40%
choices.why: Dividing total repaid by principal gives 1 + total rate (not just the rate). Subtract principal first to get interest.

73.prompt: Cost C = 2.5x + 6, Revenue R = 8x. How much does profit increase per additional item sold?

choices.label: Marginal profit = revenue per item − variable cost per item = 8 − 2.5 = $5.50 (fixed cost doesn't affect per-item change)
choices.why: Correct — Profit = R−C = 5.5x − 6. The slope 5.5 is the marginal profit. Fixed cost $6 is a one-off and doesn't repeat per item.

choices.label: Profit per item = revenue per item = $8
choices.why: Revenue ignores the $2.50 variable cost of making each item. Profit = Revenue − Cost.

choices.label: Profit per item = 8 − 2.5 − 6 = −0.5 (subtract everything including fixed cost)
choices.why: The fixed cost $6 is not per-item — it doesn't repeat with each sale. Only the variable cost (2.5) reduces each item's profit.

76.prompt: For y = 4ˣ where the base is 4 (greater than 1), what does the graph look like?

choices.label: Exponential growth: passes through (0,1), rises steeply for positive x, approaches 0 for negative x
choices.why: Correct — base > 1 means growth. At x=0: y=1. As x→−∞, y→0 (horizontal asymptote). Rises rapidly for large x.

choices.label: Exponential decay: starts high and decreases toward 0
choices.why: Decay requires 0 < base < 1. Base = 4 > 1 → growth.

choices.label: Parabola: symmetric U-shape
choices.why: Parabolas come from quadratic functions (x²). Exponential functions have x as the exponent → J-shaped curve.

77.prompt: To find the minimum spanning tree (MST) of a network, which algorithm applies?

choices.label: Kruskal's: sort edges by weight (cheapest first), add each if it doesn't form a cycle. Stop when all vertices connected.
choices.why: Correct — the MST connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight and no cycles. The last edge added is the heaviest in the MST.

choices.label: Find the longest path and remove it from the network
choices.why: MST builds up from the cheapest edges. You don't remove the longest path.

choices.label: Start at any vertex, always go to the nearest unvisited vertex (nearest-neighbour)
choices.why: Nearest-neighbour is a heuristic for the Travelling Salesman Problem — not MST. Use Kruskal's or Prim's for MST.

78.prompt: Annual leave loading of 17.5% is calculated on which base amount?

choices.label: 17.5% of the normal pay for the leave period (not the whole year)
choices.why: Correct — loading applies to ordinary leave pay only. Here: 4 weeks × $350/week = $1400 base. Loading = 17.5% of $1400 = $245.

choices.label: 17.5% of the annual salary
choices.why: Loading applies to the leave period only (e.g. 4 weeks), not the full year.

choices.label: 17.5% on top of an already-loaded amount (compound)
choices.why: Loading is a simple percentage of ordinary pay. No compounding — just 17.5% × leave pay.

79.prompt: To order 6.2×10⁻³, 4.5×10⁻⁴, and 3.2×10⁻¹ from largest to smallest, what's the quickest approach?

choices.label: Compare exponents first — less negative = larger. 10⁻¹ > 10⁻³ > 10⁻⁴, so order: 3.2×10⁻¹, 6.2×10⁻³, 4.5×10⁻⁴
choices.why: Correct — the exponent determines the order of magnitude. Only compare mantissas if exponents are equal.

choices.label: Compare mantissas only — 6.2 > 4.5 > 3.2, so 6.2×10⁻³ is largest
choices.why: Mantissas only matter when exponents are equal. 3.2×10⁻¹ = 0.32 is far larger than 6.2×10⁻³ = 0.0062.

choices.label: More negative exponent = larger value (10⁻⁴ > 10⁻¹)
choices.why: Opposite — more negative exponent = smaller value. 10⁻⁴ = 0.0001, while 10⁻¹ = 0.1. Less negative = larger.

80.prompt: To make p the subject of n = (m − p)/q, which steps are correct?

choices.label: 1. Multiply both sides by q → nq = m − p  2. Subtract m from both sides → nq − m = −p  3. Multiply by −1 → p = m − nq
choices.why: Correct — clear the denominator first (×q), then isolate p by rearranging.

choices.label: Divide both sides by q → n/q = m − p → p = m − n/q
choices.why: Dividing by q (already the denominator) doesn't clear it — multiply by q to clear the fraction.

choices.label: p = nq + m — add nq and m
choices.why: From nq = m − p, rearranging gives p = m − nq (subtract nq from both sides of nq + p = m).

81.prompt: In stratified random sampling, how many from a subgroup are selected?

choices.label: Subgroup sample = (subgroup size ÷ total population) × total sample size
choices.why: Correct — maintain proportional representation. E.g. 200/960 × 240 = 50 Year 12 students.

choices.label: Subgroup sample = total sample ÷ number of subgroups (equal splits)
choices.why: Equal splits ignore group sizes. Stratified sampling matches each group's proportion in the population.

choices.label: Subgroup sample = subgroup size − sample size
choices.why: Subtraction gives those NOT sampled. Use the proportion formula: fraction × sample size.

83.prompt: A scale model has ratio 1:64 (model:actual). The real car is 4.9m. What is the model length?

choices.label: Convert 4.9m to cm (= 490cm), then model = 490 ÷ 64 ≈ 7.7cm
choices.why: Correct — scale 1:64 means model is 64 times smaller. Convert units to match desired answer, then divide.

choices.label: Model = 4.9 × 64 = 313.6m — multiply by the scale factor
choices.why: Multiplying by 64 makes it 64× larger than real life. The model is smaller: divide by 64.

choices.label: Model = 4.9 − 64 — subtract the scale factor
choices.why: Subtracting a unitless scale factor from metres makes no sense dimensionally. Divide to apply a scale ratio.

84.prompt: Electricity: 37¢/kWh used (U), 5¢/kWh produced (P), 71¢/day fixed fee. What's the daily cost C?

choices.label: C = 71 + 37U − 5P — fixed fee + charge for use − credit for production
choices.why: Correct — costs add, credits subtract. The daily fee is independent of U and P.

choices.label: C = 71 + 37U + 5P — add production credit (it's income)
choices.why: Production earns a credit that REDUCES the bill. Subtract 5P, don't add it.

choices.label: C = (71 + 37 − 5) × (U + P) — combine rates then multiply by units
choices.why: U and P are different quantities (used vs produced). The fixed fee is per day, not per unit. Keep them separate.

85.prompt: If thickness t varies inversely with surface area A, and radius doubles (area becomes 4A), what happens to thickness?

choices.label: t is divided by 4 — area quadrupled (A = 4πr², doubling r gives ×4), so t becomes t/4
choices.why: Correct — surface area scales as r², so doubling r → ×4 area. Since t ∝ 1/A, thickness becomes t/4.

choices.label: t is divided by 2 — because radius doubled
choices.why: The area (not radius) drives the inverse. Area grows as r², so doubling r gives 4× area → t divides by 4.

choices.label: t is multiplied by 4 — larger surface needs thicker skin
choices.why: Inverse variation: more area → less thickness. The material spreads thinner as the balloon expands.

86.prompt: Game starts 3:40pm Tuesday in Quito (UTC−5). What time is it in Sydney (UTC+10)?

choices.label: Difference = UTC+10 − (UTC−5) = +15 hours. 3:40pm + 15h = 6:40am Wednesday.
choices.why: Correct — Sydney is 15 hours ahead of Quito. Add 15h: 3:40pm + 15h crosses midnight into Wednesday.

choices.label: Difference = 10 − 5 = 5 hours. 3:40pm + 5h = 8:40pm Tuesday.
choices.why: One zone is −5, not +5. The difference is 10 − (−5) = 15 hours, not 5.

choices.label: Sydney is behind Quito — subtract 15 hours: 3:40pm − 15h = 12:40am Tuesday.
choices.why: Sydney (UTC+10) is ahead of Quito (UTC−5). Add hours, don't subtract.

87.prompt: A biased 10-sided die: P(1) > P(2)=P(3)=...=P(10). Rolled 153 times, got 72 ones. Best estimate for P(10)?

choices.label: Non-ones = 153−72 = 81 rolls shared equally among faces 2-10 (9 faces). P(10) ≈ 81/(9×153) = 1/17.
choices.why: Correct — experimental probability: 81 non-one rolls spread across 9 equally-likely faces → 9 rolls each. P(10) ≈ 9/153 = 1/17.

choices.label: P(10) = 1/10 — fair die probability
choices.why: The die is biased. Use experimental data, not the theoretical fair-die probability.

choices.label: P(10) = 72/153 — fraction of one-rolls
choices.why: 72/153 estimates P(1). For face 10, use the non-one rolls: 81 non-ones ÷ 9 faces = 9, so P(10) ≈ 9/153 = 1/17.

88.prompt: M and P are equidistant from R. Bearing M from R = 017°, bearing P from R = 107°. Triangle MRP is:

choices.label: Isosceles right triangle — RM=RP (equal distances), angle at R = 107°−17° = 90°, so base angles = 45° each
choices.why: Correct — equal distances → isosceles. Angle at R equals difference in bearings: 90°. Base angles (at M and P) each = 45°.

choices.label: Equilateral — all sides and angles equal
choices.why: Equilateral requires all angles 60°. The angle at R is 90° (from the bearing difference), so it's right-isosceles, not equilateral.

choices.label: Scalene — no relationship between bearings and triangle shape
choices.why: The angle at R is precisely determined by the bearing difference (90°), and RM=RP makes it isosceles.

89.prompt: Minimum daily temperature is normally distributed with mean = SD. Zero is exactly 1 SD below the mean. What % of days are above zero?

choices.label: 84% — P(above μ−σ) = P(Z > −1) = 50% + 34% = 84% (empirical rule)
choices.why: Correct — 68% within ±1 SD means 34% in each half. Above zero (=above μ−σ=above Z=−1): 50%+34% = 84%.

choices.label: 68% — within one standard deviation
choices.why: 68% is the total within ±1 SD (both sides of mean). Above zero includes everything from Z=−1 upward = 84%.

choices.label: 16% — because zero is at the 16th percentile
choices.why: 16% is BELOW zero (i.e., below μ−σ). ABOVE zero = 100%−16% = 84%.

(a) The IQ scores for adults in City A are normally distributed with mean 108 and standard deviation 10. Yin has an IQ of 128. What percentage of adults in City A have an IQ score higher than Yin's? (2 marks)

(b) City B IQ scores are normally distributed with mean 112 and standard deviation 16. There are 1 000 000 adults in City B. Yin (IQ = 128) has moved to City B. Calculate the expected number of adults in City B with an IQ lower than Yin's. (2 marks)

writtenQuestions.answer:
(a) z = (128 − 108) / 10 = 2
Yin is 2 standard deviations above the mean.
By the 95% rule: 5% are beyond ±2 SDs → 2.5% are above.
∴ 2.5% of adults have a higher IQ than Yin.

(b) z for Yin in City B = (128 − 112) / 16 = 1
Yin is 1 SD above City B's mean.
P(IQ < 128) = 50% + 34% = 84% [68% rule → 34% between mean and +1SD]
Expected number = 0.84 × 1 000 000 = 840 000

(c) (x − 108)/10 = (x − 112)/16
16(x − 108) = 10(x − 112)
16x − 1728 = 10x − 1120
6x = 608
x = 101.3

Battery life is normally distributed: mean 840h, SD 80h. Statistical tables show 60% of batteries have life < 860h.

What percentage of batteries have a life between 820 and 920 hours?

60% below 860 → 10% between 840 and 860 (since 50% below mean).
By symmetry: 10% between 820 and 840.
68% within 1 SD (760–920) → 34% between 840 and 920.
Total between 820 and 920 = 10% + 34% = 44%.

t(t − 8) = 0
t = 0 or t = 8
The other value is t = 8.

By considering triangle OAB, calculate the area of the ten-sided shape. Give your answer in square centimetres correct to one decimal place. (4 marks)

AB = 80 ÷ 10 = 8 cm
Angle AOB = 360° ÷ 10 = 36°
Angle OAB = (180° − 36°) ÷ 2 = 72°

Using the sine rule in triangle OAB:
OA/sin(∠OBA) = AB/sin(∠AOB)
OA = 8 × sin 72°/sin 36° = 8 × 0.9511/0.5878 = 12.944 cm

Area of triangle OAB = (1/2) × OA² × sin(∠AOB) = (1/2) × 12.944² × sin 36°
= (1/2) × 167.55 × 0.5878 = 49.24 cm²

Area of decagon = 10 × 49.24 = 492.4 cm²

writtenQuestions.q: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 are each written on separate cards. Amy has cards 1, 3 and 5 and Bob has cards 2, 4 and 6. They play a game in which each person randomly chooses one of their own cards; the higher card wins. (a) A partially completed tree diagram is shown. Complete the tree diagram and find the probability that Bob wins. (2 marks) (b) Suppose Amy and Bob play this game 30 times. How many times would Bob be expected to win? (1 mark)
writtenQuestions.answer:
(a) Amy picks 1: Bob picks 2,4,6 — Bob wins all 3 → P(Bob wins | Amy=1) = 1
Amy picks 3: Bob picks 2,4,6 — Bob wins with 4,6 → P(Bob wins | Amy=3) = 2/3
Amy picks 5: Bob picks 2,4,6 — Bob wins with 6 only → P(Bob wins | Amy=5) = 1/3

P(Bob wins) = (1/3)(1) + (1/3)(2/3) + (1/3)(1/3) = 1/3 + 2/9 + 1/9 = 6/9 = 2/3

(b) Expected wins = 30 × 2/3 = 20 times

writtenQuestions.q: A wildlife park has 5 main attractions (A, B, C, D, E) connected by directional paths. The network shows the number of visitors who can access each path at any one time, with a cut shown. (a) What is the flow capacity of the cut shown? (2 marks) (c) One path is to be increased in capacity so that the overall maximum flow will be 40 visitors at any one time. Which path could be increased and by how much? (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: (a) The cut shown passes through edges: Source→A (10), Source→C (10), D→Sink (20). Cut capacity = 10 + 10 + 20 = 40. writtenQuestions.q: The diagram shows an aeroplane that was flying towards an airport at A on a bearing of 135°T. When it was at point O, 20 km away from the airport at A, the flight course was changed. The aeroplane landed at an airport at B directly south of O. The distance from O to B is 50 km. (a) Show that the distance between the airport at A and the airport at B is 38.5 km, correct to 1 decimal place. (2 marks) (b) Use the sine rule to find the angle OBA to the nearest degree. (2 marks) (c) What is the bearing of the airport at B from the airport at A? (1 mark)
writtenQuestions.answer: (a) Angle AOB = 135° − 90° = 45° (bearing 135° means A is south-east of O, so angle between north and OA is 135°, angle AOB = 135° − 90° = 45°) Using cosine rule: AB² = OA² + OB² − 2 × OA × OB × cos(∠AOB) = 20² + 50² − 2 × 20 × 50 × cos(45°) = 400 + 2500 − 2000 × 0.7071... = 2900 − 1414.2... = 1485.8... AB = √1485.8 = 38.5 km ✓ (b) Using sine rule: sin(∠OBA)/OA = sin(∠AOB)/AB sin(∠OBA)/20 = sin(45°)/38.5 sin(∠OBA) = 20 × sin(45°)/38.5 = 0.3675... ∠OBA = sin⁻¹(0.3675) ≈ 22° (c) O is due north of B. Bearing of A from B: ∠OBA = 22°, so A is 22° east of north from B. Bearing of A from B = 022°T Bearing of B from A: A is north-west of B, so bearing = 180° + 22° = 202°T

bandDescriptors.partial: Correctly applies cosine rule and sine rule but makes an error in the bearing calculation.

writtenQuestions.q: A composite solid is shown. The top section is a cylinder with height 3 cm and diameter 4 cm, centred on top of a hemisphere with diameter 6 cm. Find the total surface area of the composite solid in cm², correct to one decimal place. (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Hemisphere radius = 3 cm, cylinder radius = 2 cm

Curved surface of hemisphere = (1/2) × 4π(3²) = 18π cm²
Flat top of hemisphere minus cylinder base = π(3²) − π(2²) = 9π − 4π = 5π cm²
Curved side of cylinder = 2π × 2 × 3 = 12π cm²
Top circle of cylinder = π(2²) = 4π cm²

Total = 18π + 5π + 12π + 4π = 39π = 122.5 cm²

writtenQuestions.q: Jo is researching the relationship between the ages of teenage characters in television series and the ages of actors playing these characters. After collecting the data, Jo finds that the correlation coefficient is 0.4564. A scatterplot showing the data is drawn with the line of best fit y = −7.51 + 1.85x. Describe and interpret the data and other information provided, with reference to the context given. (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: A comprehensive response includes: Describing the data: - The relationship is linear and positive/increasing. - The correlation coefficient of 0.4564 indicates a weak to moderate positive correlation. - Character ages range from approximately 14 to 17 years; actor ages range from 14 to 30 years. Interpreting the regression equation: - The gradient of 1.85 means that as character age increases by 1 year, the actor age increases by approximately 1.85 (almost 2) years. - For each additional year of character age, actors tend to be almost 2 years older. Contextual interpretation: - Actors playing teenage characters do not need to be teenagers themselves — actors range from 14 to 30 years old for characters aged 14–17. - Characters of age 15 have the widest range of actor ages (14–27). - Characters older than 15 tend to be played by older actors. - The weak correlation shows there is considerable variation — older actors can play younger characters.

writtenQuestions.q: The diagram shows the location of three places X, Y and C. Y is 15 km from X on a bearing of 120°T. C is 40 km from X and lies due west of Y. P lies on the line joining C and Y and is due south of X. (a) Find the distance XP. (2 marks) (b) Find the bearing of C from X, to the nearest degree. (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
(a) ∠PXY = 180° − 120° = 60°
XP = XY × cos 60° = 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 km

(b) tan(∠CXP) = XC_horizontal / XP
∠PXY = 60°, so XY_horizontal = 15 × sin 60° = 12.99 km (east)
XC is west of X, so total horizontal = 12.99 + (40² − XP²)^(1/2)...

Simpler: cos(∠CXP) = XP/XC...
∠CXP: cos θ = 7.5/40... no.
Using right angle at P:
CP = XY_east = 15 sin 60° = 7.5√3 = 12.99 km
XC = √(XP² + CP²) should be 40... wait

Actually: In triangle CXP, ∠XPC = 90° (P is due south of X, C is due west of Y = west of P)
cos(∠CXP) = XP/XC = 7.5/40
∠CXP = cos⁻¹(7.5/40) = cos⁻¹(0.1875) = 79.19...° ≈ 79°

Bearing of C from X = 180° + 79° = 259°

bandDescriptors.partial: 2–3/4 — One part correct.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1/4 — ∠PXY = 60° identified.

writtenQuestions.q:
A plumber leases equipment which is valued at $60 000. The salvage value of the equipment at any time can be calculated using either of the two methods of depreciation shown in the table:
- Straight-line method: $3500 per annum
- Declining-balance method: 12% per annum

Under which method of depreciation would the salvage value of the equipment be lower at the end of 3 years? Justify your answer with appropriate mathematical calculations.
writtenQuestions.answer: Straight-line method (S = V₀ − Dn): S = $60 000 − $3500 × 3 S = $60 000 − $10 500 S = $49 500 Declining-balance method (S = V₀(1 − r)ⁿ): S = $60 000 × (1 − 12%)³ S = $60 000 × (0.88)³ S = $60 000 × 0.681472 S = $40 888.32 ∴ The declining-balance method would provide a lower salvage value ($40 888.32 < $49 500).

writtenQuestions.answer: Each ball diameter = 23 cm, radius = 11.5 cm. Surface area of sphere = 4π × (11.5)² = 4π × 132.25 = 1661.9 cm² Curved surface area of cylinder = 2π × 11.5 × 69 = 2π × 793.5 = 4985.7 − 1661.9 = ... The probability values given in the table for different values of z are represented by the shaded area in the diagram below. The scores in a university examination are normally distributed with mean 58 and standard deviation 12. (a) By calculating a z-score, find the percentage of scores that are less than 46. (2 marks) (b) Explain why the percentage of scores between 46 and 70 is twice your answer to part (a). (1 mark) (c) By using the values in the table above, find an approximate minimum score needed to be in the top 5% of this examination. (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: (a) z = (70 − 58)/15 = 12/15 = 0.8 P from table = 0.7881 P(58 to 70) = 0.7881 − 0.5 = 0.2881 = 28.81% (b) The z-score for 46: z = (46 − 58)/15 = −12/15 = −0.8 By the symmetry of the normal distribution, the area between 46 and 58 equals the area between 58 and 70. So the percentage of scores between 46 and 70 = 28.81% + 28.81% = twice the answer to (a). (c) Top 10% means P(z < Z) = 0.90. From the table, z = 1.3 gives P = 0.9032 ≈ 0.90. x = z × σ + μ = 1.3 × 15 + 58 = 19.5 + 58 = 77.5 Approximate minimum score = 77 (or 78)

A project involving nine activities is shown in the network diagram. The duration of each activity is not yet known. The following table gives the earliest start time (EST) and latest start time (LST) for three of the activities. All times are in hours.
ActivityESTLST

(a) What is the critical path? (b) The minimum time required for this project to be completed is 19 hours. What is the duration of activity I? (c) The duration of activity C is 3 hours. What is the maximum amount of time that could occur between the start of activity F and the end of activity H?
writtenQuestions.answer: (a) Activities A and C have float times (LST > EST), so they are NOT on the critical path. The critical path is BEGI. Twenty-five years ago, Phoenix deposited a single sum of money into a new bank account, earning 2.4% interest per annum compounding monthly. Present value interest factors for an annuity of $1 for various interest rates (r) and numbers of periods (n):
n \ r0.0010.0020.0030.004

Phoenix made the following withdrawals: • $2000 at the end of each month for the first 15 years (starting end of month 1) • $1200 at the end of each month for the next 10 years (starting end of month 181) Calculate the minimum sum that Phoenix could have deposited in order to make these withdrawals. (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: Monthly interest rate: r = 2.4%/12 = 0.2% = 0.002 The deposit must cover the present value of both annuities (calculated at time 0). Present value of first annuity ($2000/month for 15 years = 180 months, n=180, r=0.002): PV₁ = $2000 × 151.036 = $302 072 Wait — let me re-read the MG. MG says: - For 25 years need: 1200 × 225.430 = 270 516 (this is the PV of the SECOND annuity as if starting at t=0) - For 15 years need extra: 800 × 151.036 = 120 828.80 (extra $800/month for first 15 years) - Total = $391 344.80 The logic: Phoenix withdraws $2000 for 15 years and $1200 for the next 10 years. = $1200 for all 25 years (n=300, r=0.002) PLUS an additional $800 for the first 15 years (n=180, r=0.002) PV of $1200 for 300 months = $1200 × 225.430 = $270 516 PV of extra $800 for 180 months = $800 × 151.036 = $120 828.80 Minimum deposit = $270 516 + $120 828.80 = $391 344.80

B: ✗ (no prerequisites — starts immediately)
E: B (E follows B)

Corrected: increasing A by 2 makes A=5, so A→F→H = 5+7+5 = 17 > 16. This DOES affect the critical path.

writtenQuestions.q: A toy has a curved surface on the top which has been shaded as shown. The toy has a uniform cross-section and a rectangular base. The cross-section has heights: 6.0 cm at one edge, 3.8 cm at the midpoint (5.1 cm from each edge), and 0 cm at the other edge. The base is 10.2 cm wide and the toy is 40.0 cm long. (a) Use two applications of the trapezoidal rule to find an approximate area of the cross-section. (2 marks) (b) The total surface area of the plastic toy is 1300 cm². What percentage of the total surface area is the curved shaded surface? Give your answer correct to one decimal place. (2 marks) (c) The toy uses 1.5 g of plastic per cm³. What mass of plastic is used to make the toy? Give your answer correct to the nearest gram. (2 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
(a) Using two applications of the trapezoidal rule with h = 5.1 cm:
A ≈ (5.1/2)(6 + 3.8) + (5.1/2)(3.8 + 0)
= 2.55 × 9.8 + 2.55 × 3.8
= 24.99 + 9.69
≈ 34.68 cm²

(b) The total surface area consists of:
• Two cross-section ends: 2 × 34.68 = 69.36 cm²
• Base (rectangular bottom): 10.2 × 40 = 408 cm²
• Two side faces: 2 × (6.0 × 40) = 480 cm∂... 
Using MG: 1300 = (2 × 34.68) + (10.2 × 40) + (6 × 40) + curved surface
1300 = 69.36 + 408 + 240 + curved surface
1300 ≈ 717.36 + curved surface
Curved surface ≈ 582.64 cm²

(c) Absolute error = ½ × 0.1 cm = 0.05 cm
Percentage error = (0.05 / 10.2) × 100%
= 0.4902...×
≈ 0.490% (3 significant figures)

writtenQuestions.q: The triangle PTA is shown. The length of PA is 75 m and the length of PT is 51 m. The angle of depression from T to A is 36°, and the angle PTA is obtuse. Find the length of TA. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Since the angle of depression from T to A is 36°, the angle TAP (alternate angle) = 36° (since TA is horizontal from T’s perspective, but actually ∠TAP = 36° from the horizontal at A).

Using the sine rule to find ∠PTA:
sin(θ) / 75 = sin(36°) / 51
sin(θ) = (sin 36° × 75) / 51 = 0.8660...
θ = 59.81° ≈ 60°

Since ∠PTA is obtuse: ∠PTA = 180° − 60° = 120°

Therefore: ∠TPA = 180° − 120° − 36° = 24°

Using the sine rule:
TA / sin 24° = 51 / sin 36°
TA = (51 × sin 24°) / sin 36°
TA ≈ 35.29 m

bandDescriptors.full: Correctly identifies obtuse angle PTA = 120°, finds angle TPA = 24°, and uses sine rule to obtain TA ≈ 35.29 m.
bandDescriptors.partial: Uses sine rule correctly and identifies the obtuse angle condition. May make a minor arithmetic error.
bandDescriptors.minimal: Attempts to use the sine rule with the given information.

writtenQuestions.q: The graph shows the salvage value of a car over 5 years. The salvage values are based on the declining-balance method. The initial value is $55 000 and the value after 1 year is $44 000. By what amount will the car's value depreciate during the 10th year? (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Step 1: Find the depreciation rate r.
$44 000 = $55 000 × (1 − r)
44/55 = 1 − r
r = 1 − 44/55 = 11/55 = 0.2 = 20%

Step 2: Find the value at the end of year 9 (after 9 years of depreciation from $55 000).
Value after 9 years = $55 000 × (1 − 0.2)⁹
= $55 000 × (0.8)⁹
= $55 000 × 0.134218
= $7 381.98

Step 3: Depreciation during year 10 = value at start of year 10 × r
= $7 381.98 × 0.2
= $1 476.40

The car will depreciate by $1 476.40 during the 10th year.

bandDescriptors.full: Correctly identifies rate r = 20%, calculates value after 9 years as $7381.98, and finds depreciation in 10th year as $1476.40.
bandDescriptors.partial: Correctly finds the depreciation rate of 20% and attempts to calculate depreciation in the 10th year.
bandDescriptors.minimal: Uses the declining-balance formula or identifies the depreciation rate from the graph.

writtenQuestions.q: The diagram shows a park consisting of two equilateral triangles. The shaded triangle is a grassed section. All measurements on the diagram are in metres. The outer equilateral triangle has side length 9 m. Each vertex of the inner (shaded) triangle is located 3 m along each side of the outer triangle from a vertex. How long will it take to mow the grassed section if it takes 5 minutes to mow 20 m²? Give your answer correct to the nearest minute. (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Step 1: Find the side length c of the shaded triangle using the cosine rule.
In the triangle formed by sides 9 m and 3 m with included angle 60° (equilateral triangle angle):
c² = 9² + 3² − 2 × 9 × 3 × cos 60°
c² = 81 + 9 − 2 × 9 × 3 × 0.5
c² = 90 − 27 = 63
c = √63 ≈ 7.937 m

Step 2: Find the area of the shaded triangle.
Area = ½ × c × c × sin 60°
= ½ × 7.937 × 7.937 × sin 60°
= ½ × 63 × (√3/2)
≈ 27.28 m²

Step 3: Calculate time to mow.
Rate = 5 min per 20 m² = 0.25 min/m²
Time = 27.28 × 0.25 ≈ 6.81 minutes
≈ 7 minutes (to the nearest minute)

bandDescriptors.full: Uses cosine rule correctly to find side c ≈ 7.937 m, calculates area of shaded triangle ≈ 27.28 m², and determines mowing time ≈ 7 minutes.
bandDescriptors.partial: Correctly applies the cosine rule to find the side length and calculates the area. Minor error in final step.
bandDescriptors.minimal: Identifies that the cosine rule is needed or identifies the 60° angle in the equilateral triangle.

writtenQuestions.q: After a dose of a medication, the amount of the medication remaining in a person can be modelled by the equation y = kaˣ, where x is the number of hours after taking the dose, and y is the amount remaining in milligrams (mg). The graph shows the amount of the medication remaining in a person after x hours. Two points are shown: at x = 0, y = 15 and at x = 2, y = 9. Using the information provided, find the amount of medication that remains in a person when x = 4. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Step 1: Find k.
At x = 0: y = ka⁰ = k × 1 = k
Since y = 15 when x = 0: k = 15

Step 2: Find a.
At x = 2, y = 9:
9 = 15 × a²
a² = 9/15 = 0.6
a = √0.6 ≈ 0.7746

Step 3: Find y when x = 4.
y = 15 × (0.7746...)⁴
= 15 × 0.36
= 5.4 mg

bandDescriptors.full: Correctly identifies k = 15, finds a = √0.6 ≈ 0.7746, and calculates y = 5.4 mg when x = 4.
bandDescriptors.partial: Correctly finds k = 15 and sets up the equation to find a. Minor error in final calculation.
bandDescriptors.minimal: Recognises that k = 15 from the y-intercept or attempts to substitute given points into the equation.

writtenQuestions.q:
A car's fuel efficiency is 30 miles per US gallon.

1 US gallon = 3.8 litres (correct to 2 significant figures)
1 mile = 1.6 km (correct to 2 significant figures)

Calculate the car's fuel efficiency in litres per 100 km, correct to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer: Convert 30 miles/gallon to km/litre first: 30 miles/gallon × 1.6 km/mile ÷ 3.8 litres/gallon = 30 × 1.6 ÷ 3.8 = 48 ÷ 3.8 = 12.6315... km/litre Convert to litres/100 km: = 100 ÷ 12.6315... = 7.9 litres/100 km (to 1 d.p.)

bandDescriptors.full: Correctly converts to get 7.9 L/100 km.
bandDescriptors.partial: Converts miles to km or gallons to litres correctly in chain.
bandDescriptors.minimal: Sets up the conversion using given factors.

writtenQuestions.q: (a) In a flock of 12 600 sheep, the ratio of males to females is 1 : 20. The weights of the male sheep are normally distributed with a mean of 76.2 kg and a standard deviation of 6.8 kg. In the flock, 15 of the male sheep each weigh more than x kg. Find the value of x. (4 marks) (b) The weights of the female sheep are also normally distributed but have a smaller mean and smaller standard deviation than the weights of male sheep. Explain whether it could be expected that 300 of the females from the flock each weigh more than x kg, where x is the value found in part (a). (1 mark)
writtenQuestions.answer: (a) Total sheep = 12 600, ratio males:females = 1:20 Number of male sheep = 12 600 × (1/21) = 600 males 15 out of 600 weigh more than x kg: Proportion = 15/600 = 0.025 → P(Z > z) = 0.025 → z = 1.96 x = μ + z × σ = 76.2 + 1.96 × 6.8 = 76.2 + 13.328 = 89.528... ≈ 89.5 kg (b) Number of females = 12 600 × (20/21) = 12 000 300 out of 12 000 = 0.025 (2.5%) would need to weigh more than 89.5 kg. But females have SMALLER mean and SMALLER standard deviation than males. So x = 89.5 kg is even further into the upper tail for females. Less than 2.5% of females would weigh more than x kg. Therefore it could NOT be expected that 300 females weigh more than x kg.

bandDescriptors.full: Correctly finds 600 males, uses z=1.96, calculates x≈89.5 kg, and correctly explains females cannot reach 300.
bandDescriptors.partial: Finds number of males and sets up z-score calculation, or correctly explains part (b).
bandDescriptors.minimal: Identifies number of males (600) or states the proportion 15/600 = 0.025.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: In a flock of 12 600 sheep, the ratio of males to females is 1 : 20. The weights of the male sheep are normally distributed with a mean of 76.2 kg and a standard deviation of 6.8 kg. In the flock, 15 of the male sheep each weigh more than x kg. Find the value of x.
parts.answer: Total sheep = 12 600, ratio males:females = 1:20 Number of male sheep = 12 600 × (1/21) = 600 males 15 out of 600 weigh more than x kg: Proportion = 15/600 = 0.025 → P(Z > z) = 0.025 → z = 1.96 x = μ + z × σ = 76.2 + 1.96 × 6.8 = 76.2 + 13.328 = 89.528... ≈ 89.5 kg

bandDescriptors.partial: Attempt to use a z-score in a calculation, or equivalent merit OR Calculates the percentage of males that weigh more than x kg
bandDescriptors.minimal: Calculates the number of male sheep, or equivalent merit

parts.label: (b)
parts.q: The weights of the female sheep are also normally distributed but have a smaller mean and smaller standard deviation than the weights of male sheep. Explain whether it could be expected that 300 of the females from the flock each weigh more than x kg, where x is the value found in part (a).
parts.answer:
Number of females = 12 600 × (20/21) = 12 000
300 out of 12 000 = 0.025 (2.5%) would need to weigh more than 89.5 kg.
But females have SMALLER mean and SMALLER standard deviation than males.
So x = 89.5 kg is even further into the upper tail for females.
Less than 2.5% of females would weigh more than x kg.
Therefore it could NOT be expected that 300 females weigh more than x kg.

bandDescriptors.partial: Does not meet the criterion: provides correct reason
bandDescriptors.minimal: Does not meet the criterion: provides correct reason

boxes.heading: Substituting into formulas
boxes.html:
• Replace each letter with its given value, then follow the order of operations — multiply/divide before add/subtract, and work out anything above or below a fraction bar as its own group first
  • Keep units consistent before substituting (e.g. convert minutes to hours if the formula expects hours)

boxes.heading: Translating words into equations
boxes.html:
• Build the equation in the same order the words describe — e.g. "subtract 8, then multiply by 3" becomes 3(x − 8), not 3x − 8
  • "Is 2 more than x" means = x + 2; "is 2 less than x" means = x − 2 — the direction matters

boxes.heading: Solving linear equations
boxes.html:
• Isolate the unknown using inverse operations, applying the same operation to both sides every time
  • Undo operations in reverse order to how they were applied — undo addition/subtraction before multiplication/division

boxes.heading: Equations with fractions
boxes.html:
• Multiply every term by the denominator (or the lowest common denominator, if there's more than one) first — this clears the fraction so you're left with an ordinary linear equation
  • Don't forget to multiply terms that aren't already over a fraction too — every term on both sides needs the same multiplier

blocks.caption: Changing the subject of a formula — worked example (make x the subject of y = (ax − b)/2)

rows.label: What to do
rows.html: Multiply both sides by 2 (clear the fraction)

boxes.heading: Applying formulas in context
boxes.html:
• Real-world formulas (BAC estimation, electricity billing, wages) combine everything above: substitute known values, then solve or rearrange for whatever's unknown
  • Read carefully which letter the question wants — sometimes it's a direct substitution, other times you need to rearrange first before substituting

boxes.heading: Checking your answer
boxes.html:
• Substitute your solution back into the original equation — both sides should be equal
  • For a rearranged formula, check it still works by substituting a value for every letter and confirming both the original and rearranged versions agree

blocks.label: "Make X the subject" questions
blocks.html: Treat the target letter exactly like the unknown in an equation you're solving — undo whatever has been done to it, in reverse order, keeping both sides balanced at each step. Clear any fractions first. The multiple-choice versions of these questions are really just testing whether you did the steps in the right order.
The BAC and electricity-billing formulas here reappear as rates in M7 — Rates & Ratios — this topic teaches the algebra (substituting, rearranging), M7 covers reading and using the rate itself.

revisionQuestions.q: Given the formula A = P + Prt, find A when P = 2000, r = 0.05 and t = 3.
A student thinks of a number x. Subtracting 4 and multiplying the result by 3 gives an answer 5 more than x. Write an equation for this and solve for x.
Make x the subject of the formula y = (px + q)/4.
revisionQuestions.a: Multiply both sides by 4: 4y = px + q. Subtract q: 4y − q = px. Divide by p: x = (4y − q) ÷ p.

revisionQuestions.q: Solve the equation x + (x − 1)/3 = 7.
revisionQuestions.a: Multiply every term by 3: 3x + (x − 1) = 21 → 4x − 1 = 21 → 4x = 22 → x = 5.5.

revisionQuestions.q: The formula for BAC (males) is BAC = (10N − 7.5H) ÷ (6.8M), where N = standard drinks, H = hours drinking, M = mass in kg. Calculate the BAC for a 90 kg male who has had 6 standard drinks over 3 hours.
Explain the general strategy for making a given letter the subject of a formula.
revisionQuestions.a: Treat the target letter as the unknown you're solving for, and undo the operations applied to it in reverse order — clear any fractions by multiplying through first, then undo addition/subtraction, then undo multiplication/division, keeping both sides balanced at each step, until the target letter is alone on one side.

boxes.heading: The linear equation y = mx + c
boxes.html:
• m is the gradient (how steep the line is, and which way it slopes)
  • c is the y-intercept — the value of y when x = 0
  • To find m and c from an equation, rearrange it into y = mx + c form first — e.g. y = 5 − 3x has m = −3, c = 5

boxes.heading: Gradient — what it means
boxes.html:
• Gradient = how much y changes for every 1-unit increase in x
  • Positive gradient → line rises left to right (y increases as x increases)
  • Negative gradient → line falls left to right (y decreases as x increases)
  • Between any two points on the line: gradient = rise ÷ run = change in y ÷ change in x

boxes.heading: Building a linear model from a description
boxes.html:
• A fixed amount (a call-out fee, a base charge) becomes c, the y-intercept
  • A rate (cost per minute, per item) becomes m, the gradient
  • Combine as total = c + m × (quantity) — but check the units match first (see the exam tip below)

boxes.heading: Reading a graph's equation
boxes.html:
• Check where the line crosses the y-axis first — that's c, and it immediately rules out any candidate equation with the wrong intercept
  • Then check the slope direction (rising or falling) to confirm the sign of m, and the steepness if more than one candidate still matches

blocks.caption: Direct variation vs. a general linear relationship

rows.label: Key feature
rows.html: y is directly proportional to x — no constant term

rows.label: Graph
rows.html: Straight line shifted up/down from the origin

rows.label: Key feature
rows.html: Doesn't pass through (0, 0) unless c happens to be 0

boxes.heading: Profit as a linear model
boxes.html:
• Profit = Revenue − Cost — if both Revenue and Cost are linear in the number of items x, Profit is linear too
  • The profit gained per extra item sold is the gradient of the profit equation — i.e. Revenue's gradient minus Cost's gradient

boxes.heading: Matching graphs to equations
boxes.html:
• Eliminate options using the y-intercept first — it's usually the fastest check
  • Then use the slope direction, and finally steepness (a larger |m| means a steeper line) if more than one option remains

blocks.label: Match your units before combining rates
blocks.html: A very common trap: a rate given "per minute" combined with a variable given in hours. Convert one to match the other before substituting — e.g. "$2 per minute" for t hours of work needs 2 × 60t, not 2t.

Everything in A4 — Non-linear Relationships (parabolas, exponentials) is understood by contrast with the straight-line behaviour covered here — a constant gradient is what makes a relationship linear in the first place. Rearranging y = mx + c for m or c uses the same subject-changing skill from A1 — Formulae & Equations.

revisionQuestions.q: State the gradient and y-intercept of the line y = 5 − 3x.
revisionQuestions.a: Rewritten in y = mx + c form: y = −3x + 5. Gradient m = −3, y-intercept c = 5.

revisionQuestions.q: A plumber charges a $70 call-out fee plus $2.50 per minute. Write an equation for the total charge C, in dollars, for t hours of work.
revisionQuestions.a: t hours = 60t minutes, so C = 70 + 150t (since 2.50 × 60 = 150).

revisionQuestions.q: A line has a gradient of −4 and passes through (0, 6). Determine the y-value when x = 3.
Cost C = 4x + 20 and Revenue R = 10x for a business selling x items. Calculate how much profit increases for each additional item sold.
revisionQuestions.a: Profit = R − C = 10x − (4x + 20) = 6x − 20. The gradient is 6, so profit increases by $6 per additional item.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how to identify whether a straight-line graph represents a direct variation relationship.
revisionQuestions.a: A direct variation relationship has the form y = mx, with no constant term, so its graph is a straight line passing through the origin (0, 0). Check whether the line crosses the axes exactly at the origin — if it crosses the y-axis anywhere else, it isn't direct variation.

revisionQuestions.q: Two candidate equations are y = 2x − 3 and y = −2x − 3. The graph shown falls from left to right. Explain which equation matches.
revisionQuestions.a: A graph falling from left to right has a negative gradient. y = 2x − 3 has gradient +2 (rising), while y = −2x − 3 has gradient −2 (falling) — so y = −2x − 3 matches.

boxes.heading: Simultaneous equations (break-even & comparisons)
boxes.html:
• Two linear equations (e.g. a cost equation and a revenue equation, or two payment plans) can be compared by finding where they're equal — this is the "break-even point"
  • Solved either graphically (the intersection point of the two lines) or algebraically (set the two expressions equal and solve)
  • Before the intersection point one option is better; after it, the other is — always check which side of the break-even point the question is actually asking about

boxes.heading: Quadratic graphs — parabolas
boxes.html:
• y = ax² + bx + c — if a > 0 the parabola opens upward (a minimum turning point); if a < 0 it opens downward (a maximum turning point)
  • c is the y-intercept (the value when x = 0)
  • To recognise a parabola's graph, check which way it opens first (sign of a), then check the y-intercept matches

boxes.heading: Projectile motion (quadratics in context)
boxes.html:
• Height over time for a thrown/launched object is modelled by a downward-opening parabola, e.g. h = −5t² + 80t
  • The object is on the ground when h = 0 — this happens at the start (t = 0) and again when it lands, so solving h = 0 gives the total time in the air
  • The negative coefficient on t² reflects gravity pulling the object back down — it's always negative in these models

boxes.heading: Exponential graphs
boxes.html:
• y = a(b)ˣ — a is the starting value (at x = 0), b is the growth/decay factor
  • b > 1 → growth (curve rises, gets steeper); 0 < b < 1 → decay (curve falls, flattening toward — but never reaching — zero)
  • This is the exact same shape as F4's compound interest formula — money and populations both follow y = a(b)ˣ

blocks.caption: Recognising a graph from its equation

rows.label: Key feature
rows.html: Rises, gets steeper, never touches zero

rows.label: Key feature
rows.html: Falls, flattens toward zero, never reaches it

rows.label: Key feature
rows.html: Two curved branches, never touches either axis

boxes.heading: Direct & inverse variation
boxes.html:
• Direct variation: y varies directly with xⁿ means y = kxⁿ — if x is scaled by a factor, y is scaled by that factor raised to the power n (e.g. volume ∝ side³: doubling the side multiplies volume by 2³ = 8)
  • Inverse variation: y varies inversely with x means y = k/x, so xy = k is always constant — if x is scaled by a factor, y is divided by that same factor (e.g. double the workers, half the time)
  • To solve either type: find k from the one pair of values you're given, then substitute the new value to find the unknown

boxes.heading: Reading exponential growth/decay models
boxes.html:
• In y = a(b)ᵗ, a is always the initial value (read it off directly at t = 0 — no calculation needed)
  • The base b tells you the growth/decay rate per period: b = 1.055 means +5.5% per period; b = 0.97 means −3% per period (a decay of 3%)
  • Only the value of b determines growth vs. decay — a just sets the starting point and doesn't affect the shape

blocks.label: "Varies with" word problems
blocks.html: Whenever a question says a quantity "varies directly/inversely with" another, don't scale intuitively — write the variation equation, substitute the given pair to solve for k, then use that same k for the new situation. This is especially important for inverse variation, where doubling one quantity halves the other, not doubles it.

Exponential growth/decay here (y = a(b)ˣ) is the same structure as F4 — Investments & Loans's compound interest formula — just with different variable names. Simultaneous linear equations build on the straight-line graphs covered in A2 — Linear Relationships.

revisionQuestions.q: Determine whether the graph of y = −3x² + 2 opens upward or downward, and state whether it has a maximum or minimum turning point.
revisionQuestions.a: The coefficient of x² is negative (a = −3), so the parabola opens downward and has a maximum turning point.

revisionQuestions.q: An object's height is modelled by h = −5t² + 40t. Determine how long the object is in the air.
revisionQuestions.a: The object is at ground level when h = 0: −5t² + 40t = 0 → t(−5t + 40) = 0 → t = 0 or t = 8. It starts at t = 0 and lands at t = 8, so it is in the air for 8 seconds.

revisionQuestions.q: The number of bacteria in a culture is modelled by y = 500(1.08)ⁿ, where n is the time in minutes. State the initial number of bacteria and determine whether the population is growing or shrinking.
revisionQuestions.a: Initial number (at n = 0): y = 500(1.08)⁰ = 500. Since the base 1.08 is greater than 1, the population is growing, by 8% each minute.

revisionQuestions.q: The time to complete a task varies inversely with the number of workers. It takes 5 workers 12 hours to finish the job. Determine how long it would take 8 workers, working at the same rate.
revisionQuestions.a: Inverse variation: workers × time = k. k = 5 × 12 = 60. For 8 workers: time = 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 hours.

revisionQuestions.q: A cube's volume varies directly with the cube of its side length. Determine the factor by which the volume increases if the side length is tripled.
revisionQuestions.a: Volume ∝ side³, so tripling the side length multiplies the volume by 3³ = 27.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how to identify, from its equation alone, whether a graph shows exponential growth or exponential decay.
revisionQuestions.a: Write the equation in the form y = a × bˣ. If the base b is greater than 1, the graph shows growth (values increase); if b is between 0 and 1, it shows decay (values decrease, flattening toward zero). The value of a is just the starting value and has no effect on whether it's growth or decay — only b determines that.

boxes.heading: Earning an income
boxes.html:
• Wage — paid per hour worked; total pay varies week to week with hours (casual/part-time work)
  • Salary — a fixed annual amount, divided evenly across pay periods (e.g. fortnightly) regardless of the exact hours worked
  • Piecework — paid per item made or task completed, not per hour
  • Commission — a percentage of the value of sales made; can be tiered (a different rate applies above a threshold)
  • Royalty — a percentage of revenue paid to the creator of a work (book, song, patent) each time it is sold/used
  • Allowance — a flat extra payment for a specific condition (meal, travel, uniform) — added on top of wage, independent of hours worked

boxes.heading: Overtime & leave loading
boxes.html:
• Overtime — extra hours beyond a standard week (e.g. 38 hrs), usually paid at a higher rate: time-and-a-half = normal rate × 1.5, double time = normal rate × 2
  • Overtime pay = normal hourly rate × multiplier × overtime hours
  • Annual leave loading — an extra 17.5% paid on top of normal pay while on annual leave (compensates for lost overtime/allowances)
  • Leave loading pay = (weekly pay × weeks of leave) + 17.5% × (weekly pay × weeks of leave)

boxes.heading: Simple interest
boxes.html:
• I = P × r × t — P = principal, r = annual rate as a decimal, t = time in years
  • Interest earned/charged is the same dollar amount every year — no compounding
  • Total repaid on a simple-interest loan = P + I
  • Always convert a percentage rate to a decimal before substituting (3% → 0.03)

boxes.heading: GST & percentage discounts
boxes.html:
• GST is 10% of the pre-GST price, so a GST-inclusive price = pre-GST price × 1.1
  • To find the GST already included in a GST-inclusive price: GST = price ÷ 11 (since 10/110 = 1/11)
  • Successive discounts don't add up directly — apply each discount to the reduced price in turn, e.g. 30% then 20% off leaves 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the original, a total discount of 44%, not 50%

rows.label: Formula
rows.html:
S = V₀ − D × n
D = loss per period, n = number of periods

rows.label: When it's used
rows.html: A fixed dollar amount is lost each period (or per km driven) — the same amount every time

rows.label: Formula
rows.html:
S = V₀ × (1 − r)ⁿ
r = rate per period as a decimal, n = number of periods

rows.label: When it's used
rows.html: A fixed percentage of the current value is lost each period — the dollar loss shrinks over time since it's a % of a smaller base

boxes.heading: Income tax & PAYG
boxes.html:
• Taxable income = gross income − allowable deductions (e.g. work expenses, union fees)
  • Tax payable is worked out from a tax bracket table given in the question — always in the form "base amount + c¢ for each $1 over a threshold"
  • Medicare levy — usually 2% of taxable income, added on top of income tax
  • PAYG (Pay As You Go) — tax withheld from each pay by the employer and sent to the ATO progressively through the year, as an estimate of what will be owed
  • Refund vs. owing — compare total PAYG withheld to actual tax payable: PAYG > tax payable → refund; PAYG < tax payable → the taxpayer owes the shortfall

boxes.heading: Shares & investments
boxes.html:
• Profit/loss = (selling price − buying price) × number of shares − brokerage fees
  • Brokerage — a fee charged by the broker for handling the transaction, usually charged on both the buy and the sell — it reduces profit, don't forget to subtract it
  • Shares can also be compared to fixed-rate investments using percentage return over time

blocks.label: Reading financial word problems
blocks.html: These questions pack a lot into one sentence — before calculating, underline: is the amount weekly or annual? Is a price GST-inclusive or exclusive? Is a rate per annum or per period? Getting one of these wrong flips the whole answer, even if your formula and arithmetic are correct.

Simple interest and straight-line depreciation are the "flat-rate" versions of ideas that reappear in compound growth — see F4 — Investments & Loans for compound interest (A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ) and reducing-balance loans, which use the same declining-balance logic as this topic's depreciation.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the difference between a wage and a salary.
revisionQuestions.a: A wage is paid per hour worked, so total pay can vary week to week depending on hours. A salary is a fixed annual amount, divided evenly into regular pay instalments (e.g. fortnightly) regardless of the exact hours worked in that period.

revisionQuestions.q: Calculate the simple interest earned on $4000 invested at 2.5% p.a. for 3 years.
A courier van worth $48 000 new depreciates at $0.18 per km driven, using the straight-line method. Find its value after it has travelled 90 000 km.
Describe what determines whether a taxpayer receives a refund or owes money at the end of the financial year.
revisionQuestions.a: Throughout the year the employer withholds PAYG tax as an estimate of what will be owed. At tax time, the taxpayer's actual tax payable — calculated from their annual taxable income using the tax bracket table — is compared to the total PAYG withheld. If PAYG paid is more than the tax payable, the difference is refunded; if it's less, the taxpayer must pay the shortfall.

revisionQuestions.q: An item is priced at $253, GST inclusive. Determine the amount of GST included in this price.
revisionQuestions.a: The GST-inclusive price is 11/10 of the pre-GST price, so the GST component is 1/11 of the total: GST = 253 ÷ 11 = $23.

revisionQuestions.q: A salesperson earns a base salary plus 2% commission on sales up to $500 000 and 3% on any amount above that. Explain how to calculate their total pay for sales of $650 000.
revisionQuestions.a: Commission = (2% × $500 000) + (3% × ($650 000 − $500 000)) = $10 000 + $4 500 = $14 500. This is added to the base salary for total pay — the higher 3% rate only applies to the portion of sales above the $500 000 threshold, not the whole sale amount.

boxes.heading: Compound interest — future value
boxes.html:
• A = P(1 + r/n)nt — P = principal, r = annual rate as a decimal, n = number of times compounded per year, t = time in years
  • Unlike simple interest, each period's interest is calculated on the current balance (principal + interest already earned), not just the original principal
  • Match the rate and the number of periods carefully — e.g. "8% p.a. compounded quarterly for 6 years" means r = 0.08, n = 4, t = 6, so nt = 24 periods

boxes.heading: Finding the present value
boxes.html:
• PV = FV ÷ (1 + r/n)nt — rearranges the future value formula to answer "how much do I need to invest now?"
  • Use this whenever a question gives you a target future amount and asks for the starting investment, rather than the other way around
  • The rate, compounding frequency and time work exactly the same way as in the future value formula — only the unknown moves

boxes.heading: Shares & dividends
boxes.html:
• Dividend yield = (annual dividend per share ÷ share price) × 100% — lets you compare returns between shares of very different prices
  • A higher dividend yield means a better return relative to what was paid for the share, even if the dollar dividend or share price alone looks smaller
  • Profit/loss on buying and selling shares still follows F1's rule: (selling price − buying price) × number of shares − brokerage fees

boxes.heading: Appreciation (growth in value)
boxes.html:
• Some assets (antiques, some property, some collectables) gain value over time instead of depreciating
  • Uses the same compound-growth shape as interest: Value after t years = V₀(1 + r)ᵗ
  • The only difference from compound interest is what's growing — dollars in an account vs. the value of an item — the maths is identical

blocks.caption: Compound interest formula — what each symbol means

rows.label: Meaning
rows.html: Annual interest rate, as a decimal

rows.label: Meaning
rows.html: Number of times compounded per year

boxes.heading: Declining-balance depreciation
boxes.html:
• Same formula as F1's declining-balance method — S = V₀(1 − r)ⁿ — but F4 questions often give the rate per half-year or per quarter rather than per year
  • Match n to whatever period the rate is given in — "8% per half-year for 5 years" means r = 0.08 and n = 10 (not 5)

boxes.heading: Reducing-balance loans
boxes.html:
• Each repayment is split between interest (charged on the amount currently owed) and paying down the principal
  • Interest is largest early in the loan, when the balance owing is still close to the original amount — so early repayments reduce the principal only a little
  • As the balance falls, less of each fixed repayment is needed for interest, so more goes toward the principal — the loan pays down faster later on

boxes.heading: Credit cards
boxes.html:
• Interest usually compounds daily on the amount owing
  • Many cards offer an interest-free period (e.g. 45 days) — pay the full balance within it and no interest is charged at all
  • If any amount is still owing after the interest-free period, interest starts accruing on the outstanding balance from that point (or from the purchase date, depending on the card's terms) until it's repaid

boxes.heading: Comparing investment options
boxes.html:
• When a question offers two different schemes (e.g. a lump sum vs. regular deposits, or different compounding frequencies), calculate the future value of each separately using its own method/formula
  • Never assume the higher quoted rate or the more frequent compounding automatically wins — compare the actual calculated totals

blocks.label: Matching variables to the question
blocks.html: Before substituting into any formula on this page, write out what P, r, n and t actually are in the question. The most common error isn't the formula — it's using the wrong n (e.g. forgetting to convert an annual rate when compounding is quarterly) or mixing up which value is being asked for (future value vs. present value vs. the rate itself).

These formulas build directly on F1 — Money Matters: compound interest is the "reinvesting" version of F1's simple interest, and declining-balance depreciation here uses the exact same formula as F1, just often with a per-period (not per-year) rate.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why compound interest results in a greater final amount than simple interest for the same principal, rate and time.
revisionQuestions.a: Simple interest earns the same dollar amount each year, calculated only on the original principal. Compound interest recalculates the interest each period on the current balance — principal plus all interest already earned — so the amount earning interest keeps growing. This compounding effect means compound interest overtakes simple interest for the same rate and time, and the gap grows the longer the investment runs.

revisionQuestions.q: Calculate the future value of $5000 invested at 6% p.a. compounded quarterly for 3 years.
A painting bought for $8000 appreciates at 4% p.a. Find its value after 6 years.

Company A has a share price of $18.20 and pays a dividend of $1.10 per share. Company B has a share price of $6.40 and pays $0.52 per share. Determine which is the better investment based on dividend yield.
revisionQuestions.a: Dividend yield = (dividend ÷ share price) × 100%. Company A: (1.10 ÷ 18.20) × 100 ≈ 6.04%. Company B: (0.52 ÷ 6.40) × 100 = 8.125%. Company B has the higher dividend yield, so it gives a better return relative to its price — even though Company A's dividend and share price are both larger in dollar terms.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why, in the early years of a reducing-balance loan, a large portion of each repayment goes toward interest rather than reducing the principal.
revisionQuestions.a: Interest each period is calculated on the current amount owing. Early in the loan the balance is still close to the original amount borrowed, so the interest charge is largest at that point — meaning most of each fixed repayment covers that interest, leaving only a small remainder to reduce the principal. As the balance falls over time, the interest portion shrinks and more of each repayment goes toward paying down the principal.

revisionQuestions.q: A credit card has a 45-day interest-free period and charges 15% p.a. compounded daily after that. Describe what determines whether interest is charged on a purchase.
revisionQuestions.a: If the cardholder pays the full balance within the 45-day interest-free period, no interest is charged on that purchase at all. If any amount remains unpaid once the period ends, interest begins compounding daily on the outstanding balance from that point until it is fully repaid.

boxes.heading: What is an annuity?
boxes.html:
• A sequence of equal, regular payments into (or out of) an account that earns compound interest each period
  • Payments are usually made at the end of each compounding period
  • Can work either way: building up savings (regular deposits) or paying off a loan (regular repayments)

boxes.heading: Recurrence relations for annuities
boxes.html:
• Aₙ = Aₙ₋₁ × (1 + r) ± payment — r is the interest rate per period, A₀ is the starting balance
  • Add the payment for an investment (regular deposits growing the balance)
  • Subtract the payment for a loan or a withdrawal (regular amounts drawn down)
  • Work through one period at a time — there's no shortcut, just repeat the same step

boxes.heading: Future value of an annuity (using tables)
boxes.html:
• Exams provide a "future value of an annuity of $1" table — look up the factor for the given rate and number of periods
  • FV = payment × (FV interest factor) — multiply the table value by the actual payment amount

boxes.heading: Present value of an annuity (using tables)
boxes.html:
• Same idea with a "present value of an annuity of $1" table
  • PV = payment × (PV interest factor) — used to value a future stream of payments in today's dollars, or to connect a loan amount to its repayments

rows.label: What the table gives you
rows.html: The value $1 invested each period grows to by the end

rows.label: What the table gives you
rows.html: Today's value of $1 to be paid each period

rows.label: What the table gives you
rows.html: Same PV factor, rearranged to solve for the unknown repayment

boxes.heading: Loans repaid via annuity tables
boxes.html:
• A reducing-balance loan repaid in equal instalments is mathematically an annuity in reverse — the loan amount is the present value of all the future repayments
  • Repayment = loan amount ÷ PV interest factor — using the factor for the loan's rate per period and total number of repayments

boxes.heading: PV vs. FV — which is bigger
boxes.html:
• For any annuity: PV < total of the nominal (face-value) payments < FV
  • Discounting brings future payments back to a smaller value today (PV); compounding grows the account to more than the sum of the plain contributions (FV)

blocks.label: Matching the table to the question
blocks.html: Always match the interest factor table's rate-per-period and number-of-periods to the question's actual compounding frequency — e.g. monthly repayments need the monthly rate and the total number of months, not the annual figures. Reading the wrong row/column of the table is the single most common error in this topic.
Annuities extend F4 — Investments & Loans's single-lump-sum compound interest to a whole series of regular payments — the underlying compounding is identical, just applied repeatedly.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the difference between the future value and the present value of an annuity.
revisionQuestions.a: The future value (FV) is the total amount accumulated at the end of the annuity's term — every payment plus all the compound interest earned. The present value (PV) is the equivalent single lump sum, invested today, that would grow into (or is needed to fund) that same stream of payments. PV is always smaller than FV, since it hasn't yet had the chance to earn interest.

revisionQuestions.q: A savings recurrence relation is Aₙ = Aₙ₋₁ × 1.004 − 250, with A₀ = $10 000. Find the balance after the second withdrawal (A₂).
An annuity has a future value interest factor of 12.0061 for 10 yearly payments at a given rate. If each payment is $2000, calculate the future value of the annuity.
A loan of $180 000 is to be repaid in equal monthly instalments. The present value interest factor for the loan's rate and term is 150.30. Calculate the monthly repayment.
revisionQuestions.a: Repayment = loan amount ÷ PV factor = 180 000 ÷ 150.30 ≈ $1197.61.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why, for the same regular payment amount, the present value of an annuity is always less than the total of all the nominal (undiscounted) payments.
revisionQuestions.a: The present value discounts every future payment back to today's value using the interest rate — money received in the future is worth less today, since it hasn't yet had the chance to earn interest. So even though the actual dollar payments add up to a certain total, their combined value today (PV) is always less than that simple total.

revisionQuestions.q: Describe, in general terms, how a recurrence relation for an annuity differs between an investment (building up savings) and a loan (paying down debt).
revisionQuestions.a: In both cases the balance is multiplied by (1 + r) each period to add interest. For an investment, the regular contribution is added each period, so the balance grows from both interest and new deposits. For a loan, the regular repayment is subtracted each period — interest still accrues on the balance (working against the borrower), but the repayment reduces it, so the balance shrinks over time as long as repayments exceed the interest charged.

boxes.heading: Accuracy & percentage error
boxes.html:
• No measurement is exact — it's accurate to half the smallest unit used, e.g. a length given "to the nearest cm" carries an error of ±0.5 cm
  • Percentage error = (limit of accuracy ÷ measured value) × 100% — smaller relative to a bigger measured value means a smaller percentage error, even if the absolute error is the same

boxes.heading: Significant figures & standard form
boxes.html:
• Leading zeros are never significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are
  • Standard form: a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 — a very small number has a large negative exponent
  • To order numbers in standard form, compare the exponents first — only compare the a values if the exponents are equal

boxes.heading: Upper & lower bounds
boxes.html:
• When two rounded measurements are combined (e.g. multiplied for area), the bounds don't combine directly
  • To find the minimum result, use the minimum value of every measurement; for the maximum, use every maximum value
  • E.g. a rectangle measured 8 cm × 5 cm to the nearest cm: min area = 7.5 × 4.5, max area = 8.5 × 5.5

boxes.heading: Perimeter of common & composite shapes
boxes.html:
• Rectangle 2(l+w) · Square 4s · Triangle a+b+c · Circle circumference = πd = 2πr
  • For a composite shape's perimeter, only count the actual outer boundary — don't include any internal join lines between the shapes making it up

rows.label: Formula
rows.html: A = ½(a+b)h — a, b are the two parallel sides

rows.label: Formula
rows.html: A = (θ/360) × πr² — θ is the sector angle in degrees

boxes.heading: Volume of solids — building blocks
boxes.html:
• Prism (any cross-section): V = A×h — cross-sectional area × the length/height perpendicular to it
  • Cylinder: V = πr²h
  • Cone: V = 1⁄3πr²h
  • Pyramid: V = 1⁄3 × base area × h
  • Sphere: V = 4⁄3πr³

boxes.heading: Composite solids — combining volumes
boxes.html:
• Split the solid into simple shapes from the list above, then add volumes for stacked/joined pieces (e.g. a cone on a cylinder, a hemisphere on a cylinder) or subtract for a hollow/cut-out piece
  • Watch for a hemisphere — it's exactly half a sphere's volume, ½ × 4⁄3πr³
  • Make sure every piece uses the same radius where they join (e.g. a cylinder and the cone/hemisphere sitting on top of it)

boxes.heading: Scale drawings
boxes.html:
• A scale like 1 : 3000 means 1 unit on the drawing = 3000 of the same unit in real life — multiply a drawn length by the scale factor to get the real length
  • Area scales by the square of the linear scale factor — real area = drawn area × (scale factor)². This is the most common thing to forget: don't just multiply area by the scale factor once

boxes.heading: The trapezoidal rule
boxes.html:
• Estimates the area of an irregular region from a series of equally spaced parallel measurements y₀, y₁, y₂, …
  • For 2 strips (3 measurements): Area ≈ (h/2)(y₀ + 2y₁ + y₂) — h is the common width between measurements; every "interior" reading is doubled, only the first and last are counted once
  • Used for things like a block of land or a cross-section that isn't a standard shape

boxes.heading: Capture–recapture (Lincoln index)
boxes.html:
• Estimates a population too large to count directly (e.g. fish in a lake)
  • Capture and tag a sample of size n₁, release them, then later capture a second sample of size n₂ and count how many are tagged (m)
  • Estimated population N ≈ (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m — assumes tagged individuals mix back in evenly and the population doesn't change between samples

boxes.heading: Circle segments & basic trigonometry
boxes.html:
• For a chord across a circle (e.g. the water surface in a pipe), use Pythagoras with the radius, half the chord length, and the distance from the centre to the chord: r² = (½ chord)² + distance² — rearrange for whichever length is unknown
  • In a right-angled triangle with a known hypotenuse and angle: opposite = hypotenuse × sin(angle), adjacent = hypotenuse × cos(angle)

blocks.label: Composite shapes and solids
blocks.html: Before calculating anything, sketch the shape or solid and label which simple pieces it's built from — then decide whether you're adding them (stacked or joined) or subtracting (a hole or cut-out). Most errors on these questions come from mixing up which operation applies, not from the formulas themselves.

Rounding, accuracy and percentage error covered here apply throughout the course — whenever a written question gives you a measured or scaled value, check what level of precision (decimal places or significant figures) the question expects in your final answer.

revisionQuestions.q: A length is measured as 24.0 cm, correct to one decimal place. Calculate the percentage error in this measurement.
revisionQuestions.a: Limit of accuracy = ±0.05 cm (half of the smallest unit, 0.1 cm). Percentage error = (0.05 ÷ 24.0) × 100% ≈ 0.21%.

revisionQuestions.q: A rectangle's sides are measured as 9 cm and 6 cm, both to the nearest centimetre. Find the upper and lower bounds for its area.
revisionQuestions.a: Each measurement has a bound of ±0.5 cm. Minimum area = 8.5 × 5.5 = 46.75 cm². Maximum area = 9.5 × 6.5 = 61.75 cm².

revisionQuestions.q: A composite solid is a cone (radius 4 cm, height 9 cm) sitting on top of a cylinder with the same radius and height 12 cm. Calculate its total volume, correct to one decimal place.
revisionQuestions.a: Cylinder: V = πr²h = π(4)²(12) ≈ 603.2 cm³. Cone: V = ⅓πr²h = ⅓π(4)²(9) ≈ 150.8 cm³. Total = 603.2 + 150.8 ≈ 754.0 cm³.

revisionQuestions.q: A map has a scale of 1 : 2000. A park is drawn on the map with an area of 3 cm². Calculate the real area of the park in m².
revisionQuestions.a: Linear scale factor is 2000, so area scales by 2000² = 4 000 000. Real area = 3 × 4 000 000 = 12 000 000 cm² = 1200 m² (dividing by 10 000 to convert cm² to m²).

revisionQuestions.q: A researcher tags 60 turtles and releases them back into a bay. Two weeks later, she catches 45 turtles and finds 9 are tagged. Estimate the total turtle population in the bay.
revisionQuestions.a: N ≈ (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m = (60 × 45) ÷ 9 = 300 turtles.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why the trapezoidal rule only gives an estimate of area, not an exact value.
revisionQuestions.a: The trapezoidal rule approximates the region between each pair of measurements as a straight-sided trapezium. If the actual boundary curves between those measurement points, the straight edge doesn't match the true shape exactly, so the calculated area differs slightly from the real area — the estimate improves as more, closer-together measurements are used.

boxes.heading: Longitude & time zones
boxes.html:
• Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 15° of longitude = 1 hour of time difference
  • Moving east makes the local time later (ahead); moving west makes it earlier (behind) — Earth rotates west to east, so eastern places reach each new hour first
  • UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) is the reference point — a city at UTC+10 is 10 hours ahead of UTC; a city at UTC−5 is 5 hours behind

boxes.heading: Latitude & north/south position
boxes.html:
• Latitude measures position north or south of the equator (0°), up to 90° at each pole
  • Moving "north" from a southern latitude reduces the °S value — moving far enough north can cross the equator into °N (e.g. 20°S + 55° north = 35°N)
  • Latitude affects position, not time — a longitude question is what actually determines the time-zone calculation

boxes.heading: Calculating the time in another zone
boxes.html:
• Find the difference in UTC offset between the two zones (e.g. UTC+10 vs. UTC−5 → 15 hours apart)
  • Add that difference to move to a zone further east (ahead); subtract it to move to a zone further west (behind)

boxes.heading: Handling the date
boxes.html:
• If adding or subtracting hours pushes the time past midnight in either direction, the day changes too
  • Track this carefully — crossing midnight forward means the next day; crossing it backward means the previous day

blocks.caption: Worked example — City A (UTC+10) is 8:00 pm Wed. What's the time in City B (UTC−5)?

rows.label: Result
rows.html: City A is 15 hours ahead of City B

rows.label: What to do
rows.html: Subtract 15 hours from City A's time (moving to the zone behind)

boxes.heading: Flight duration across time zones
boxes.html:
• The safest method: 1) convert the departure local time to UTC (remove the departure zone's offset), 2) add the flight duration, 3) convert that UTC time to the destination zone's local time (apply the destination's offset)
  • Working through UTC avoids sign errors from jumping directly between two local times, especially when the zones have opposite-sign offsets

boxes.heading: Reverse problems
boxes.html:
• If given the arrival time and flight duration, and asked for the departure time: convert arrival local time to UTC, subtract the flight duration, then convert that UTC time to the departure zone's local time
  • Same method as forward problems, just run in reverse

blocks.label: Work through UTC, not zone-to-zone directly
blocks.html: Always convert to UTC first, do the arithmetic there, then convert to whichever zone the question asks for — rather than trying to jump directly from one local time to another. This is especially important when the two zones have opposite-sign offsets (one east of UTC, one west).
Flight-duration problems combine this topic's time-zone conversion with the elapsed-time reading covered in M7 — Rates & Ratios's speed/distance/time work.
