revisionQuestions.q: Explain why moving east across time zones makes the local time later, while moving west makes it earlier.
revisionQuestions.a: Earth rotates from west to east, so places further east reach sunrise — and each new hour — before places to the west. This means a location east of you is ahead in time (a later clock reading at the same instant), and a location west of you is behind (an earlier clock reading).

revisionQuestions.q: A meeting starts at 4:00 pm Tuesday in a city at UTC+8. Determine the time and day in a city at UTC−3 at that same instant.
revisionQuestions.a: Offset difference = 8 − (−3) = 11 hours; the UTC+8 city is 11 hours ahead. Subtract 11 hours from 4:00 pm Tuesday: 4:00 pm − 11 h = 5:00 am Tuesday.

revisionQuestions.q: A flight departs Sydney (UTC+10) at 11:30 pm Monday and takes 14 hours 45 minutes to reach Los Angeles (UTC−8). Determine the arrival time and day in Los Angeles.
revisionQuestions.a: Convert departure to UTC: 11:30 pm Mon − 10 h = 1:30 pm Mon UTC. Add flight duration: 1:30 pm Mon + 14 h 45 min = 4:15 am Tue UTC. Convert to LA (UTC−8): 4:15 am Tue − 8 h = 8:15 pm Monday in Los Angeles.

revisionQuestions.q: City P is at latitude 20°S. City Q is 55° north of City P. State the latitude of City Q.
revisionQuestions.a: Moving 55° north from 20°S crosses the equator: 55 − 20 = 35°N.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the general method for solving a time-zone problem that involves a long flight duration, to minimise the risk of errors.
revisionQuestions.a: Convert the departure local time into UTC by removing the departure city's offset. Add the flight's duration to that UTC time. Then convert the resulting UTC time into the destination city's local time by applying its offset. Working through UTC at every step avoids the confusion of jumping directly between two local times, especially when the offsets have different signs.

revisionQuestions.q: A game starts at 6:15 am Saturday in a city at UTC−4. Determine the time and day in a city at UTC+9 at that same instant.
revisionQuestions.a: Offset difference = 9 − (−4) = 13 hours ahead. Add 13 hours to 6:15 am Saturday: 6:15 am + 13 h = 7:15 pm Saturday.

boxes.heading: The sine rule
boxes.html:
• a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC — each side is paired with the angle opposite it
  • Use it when you know an angle-side opposite pair, plus one more angle or side
  • Ambiguous case: solving for an angle can give two valid answers (acute and obtuse), since sin(θ) = sin(180° − θ) — check which fits the rest of the triangle (angle sum = 180°, or a stated condition like "obtuse")

boxes.heading: The cosine rule
boxes.html:
• c² = a² + b² − 2ab cosC — finds an unknown side when you know the other two sides and the included angle
  • Rearranged, cosC = (a² + b² − c²) ÷ (2ab) — finds an unknown angle when all three sides are known

boxes.heading: Area of a triangle
boxes.html: • Area = ½ab sinC — two sides and the included angle between them (doesn't need a right angle or the base/height)

boxes.heading: Choosing the right rule
boxes.html:
• Right angle present → Pythagoras / SOH-CAH-TOA is usually simplest
  • 2 sides + included angle, need the 3rd side or the area → cosine rule or area formula
  • 3 sides known, need an angle → cosine rule (rearranged)
  • An angle-side opposite pair + one more piece → sine rule

boxes.heading: Bearings
boxes.html:
• True bearing: measured clockwise from north, always written as 3 digits (000°–360°)
  • A compass bearing like S48°W converts to a true bearing by measuring from the stated north/south direction toward east or west

boxes.heading: Compound bearing problems
boxes.html:
• The angle between two bearings measured from the same point is the difference between them (adjust if the angle needed crosses 000°/360°)
  • Sketch first: draw a north line at every point mentioned, mark the given bearings and distances, then identify the triangle before choosing sine rule, cosine rule, or the area formula

blocks.label: Sketch before you calculate
blocks.html: For any bearings or non-right-angled triangle problem, draw a labelled diagram first — mark north at each relevant point, write in every known side and angle, and identify which triangle you're actually solving. Most errors in this topic come from misreading the diagram's angles, not from applying the wrong formula.
This topic builds directly on the basic right-triangle trigonometry (SOH-CAH-TOA, Pythagoras) introduced in M1 — Measurement, extending it to triangles that don't have a right angle.

revisionQuestions.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 10 cm, angle A = 40°, angle B = 65°. Use the sine rule to find the length of BC, correct to 1 decimal place.
revisionQuestions.a: Angle C = 180° − 40° − 65° = 75°. BC/sinA = AB/sinC → BC = 10 × sin40° ÷ sin75° ≈ 6.7 cm.

revisionQuestions.q: In triangle PQR, PQ = 8 cm, QR = 6 cm, angle PQR = 110°. Use the cosine rule to find PR, correct to 1 decimal place.
A triangle has sides a = 7, b = 9, c = 12. Use the cosine rule to find the size of the angle opposite side c, correct to the nearest degree.
Calculate the area of a triangle with two sides of 9 cm and 14 cm, and an included angle of 52°, correct to 1 decimal place.
A ship sails from port on a bearing of 048°T for 20 km, then changes course to a bearing of 138°T for 15 km. Explain how to find the angle between the two legs of the journey at the turning point.
revisionQuestions.a: The angle between two bearings measured from the same point is the difference between them: 138° − 48° = 90°, so the two legs meet at a right angle at the turning point. This angle, together with the two known distances, allows the cosine rule to find the direct distance back to port.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why the sine rule can sometimes give two possible answers for an unknown angle (the ambiguous case), and how to decide which is correct.
revisionQuestions.a: Because sin(θ) = sin(180° − θ), an angle and its supplement have the same sine value — so solving the sine rule for an angle can produce both an acute and an obtuse solution. The correct one is chosen by checking which is consistent with the rest of the triangle: the three angles must sum to 180°, and the question may explicitly state that a particular angle is obtuse.

boxes.heading: Ratios — simplifying, dividing & changing
boxes.html:
• Simplify a ratio by dividing every term by their highest common factor
  • To divide a quantity in a given ratio: total parts = sum of the ratio numbers, then each share = (quantity ÷ total parts) × that number
  • Both quantities in a ratio must be in the same units before simplifying — e.g. "20 minutes to one-third of a day" needs converting to the same unit (minutes) first
  • If amounts are added or removed (e.g. jelly beans eaten, liquid removed from a mixture), calculate the new individual amounts first, then re-simplify the ratio from those — don't adjust the ratio numbers directly

boxes.heading: Scale (model : actual)
boxes.html:
• A scale of 1 : n means 1 unit on the model/map = n of the same unit in real life
  • Model → actual: multiply by n. Actual → model: divide by n
  • Convert units at the end, not the start — work in one consistent unit throughout the ratio calculation, then convert the answer if the question asks for a different unit

boxes.heading: Speed, distance & time
boxes.html:
• Speed = distance ÷ time, so distance = speed × time, and time = distance ÷ speed
  • Convert time to match the speed's units before dividing — e.g. "3 hours 30 minutes" must become 3.5 hours to use with km/h
  • Reading start/end clock times (e.g. 6:42 am to 8:04 am) — find the elapsed time first, converting to hours as a decimal if needed

boxes.heading: Best value (unit pricing)
boxes.html:
• Unit price = cost ÷ quantity — the lower unit price is the better deal
  • All options must be compared in the same unit (e.g. cost per litre, cost per 100 g) — convert first if the options are given in different sizes

boxes.heading: Rates of change (linear)
boxes.html:
• Some quantities change by a fixed amount per unit of time — e.g. blood alcohol concentration (BAC) decreasing by a set amount per hour — the same "flat rate" structure as F1's straight-line depreciation
  • To find the time to reach a target value: time = (starting value − target value) ÷ rate of change

boxes.heading: Using a rate to estimate a total
boxes.html:
• Count/measure a small, representative sample (e.g. trees in a small section of land), and calculate the rate for that sample (e.g. trees per m²)
  • Scale up: multiply the rate by the total area/quantity to estimate the full total — this assumes the sample is spread evenly and is genuinely representative
  • Capture–recapture (tagging and resampling to estimate an animal population) uses this same idea, applied to a ratio of tagged-to-total in each sample — see M1 — Measurement for the full method

blocks.label: Units, units, units
blocks.html: Almost every mistake in this topic comes from mismatched units — minutes vs. hours, cm vs. m, or comparing a 1.5 L price against a 2 L price without converting to a common unit first. Before calculating, check every quantity in the question is in the same unit you need for the formula.

Scale here uses the same ratio idea as F1/F4's money problems and M1's scale drawings — the difference is just what's being scaled (a length or a price, not an area). Capture-recapture population estimation is covered in full under M1 — Measurement.

revisionQuestions.q: A drink is made from cordial and water in the ratio 1 : 4. Determine how much cordial is needed to make 3 L of the drink.
revisionQuestions.a: Total parts = 1 + 4 = 5. Cordial = (1 ÷ 5) × 3 L = 0.6 L.

revisionQuestions.q: A car travels 210 km in 3 hours 30 minutes. Calculate its average speed in km/h.
revisionQuestions.a: Convert time to hours: 3 h 30 min = 3.5 h. Speed = distance ÷ time = 210 ÷ 3.5 = 60 km/h.

revisionQuestions.q: Two bottles of juice are for sale: a 1.5 L bottle for $4.50, and a 2 L bottle for $5.60. Determine which is better value.
revisionQuestions.a: Unit price: 1.5 L bottle = $4.50 ÷ 1.5 = $3.00/L. 2 L bottle = $5.60 ÷ 2 = $2.80/L. The 2 L bottle is better value, since its price per litre is lower.

revisionQuestions.q: A model bridge is built at a scale of 1 : 150. Calculate the real length, in metres, of a section that measures 8 cm on the model.
revisionQuestions.a: Real length = 8 cm × 150 = 1200 cm = 12 m.

revisionQuestions.q: A person's BAC is 0.090 at midnight and decreases at a constant rate of 0.012 per hour. Calculate how long it takes for their BAC to reach zero.
revisionQuestions.a: Time = starting value ÷ rate = 0.090 ÷ 0.012 = 7.5 hours.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain how a small sample can be used to estimate the number of trees on a large block of land.
revisionQuestions.a: Count the trees in a small, representative section of the block, then calculate the rate (trees per unit area, e.g. trees per m²) for that section. Multiply this rate by the total area of the block to estimate the total number of trees — this assumes the trees are spread roughly evenly across the whole block.

boxes.heading: Networks — the basics
boxes.html:
• A vertex is a point/node; an edge is a connection between two vertices
  • A weighted edge has a number attached — a distance, time, cost or capacity
  • Only which vertices connect to which matters — the exact shape a network is drawn in doesn't change what it represents

boxes.heading: Degree of a vertex
boxes.html:
• The degree of a vertex is the number of edges connected to it
  • Sum of all degrees = 2 × number of edges — every edge is counted at both of the vertices it connects, so the total degree is always even

boxes.heading: Complete bipartite networks (round-robins)
boxes.html:
• If every member of one group must connect to every member of a second group exactly once (with no connections within either group), it's a complete bipartite network
  • Total edges = (size of group 1) × (size of group 2) — e.g. a chess round-robin between a 3-person team and a 4-person team has 3 × 4 = 12 games

boxes.heading: Counting handshakes (a complete network)
boxes.html:
• If everyone in a group of n people connects to every other person exactly once, total connections = n(n−1)/2
  • This is different from the bipartite case — here everyone is in one single group, connecting to everyone else

rows.label: Situation
rows.html: Group of size p vs. group of size q, each connects to every member of the other once

rows.label: Situation
rows.html: n people, everyone connects to everyone else once

boxes.heading: Minimum spanning tree (MST)
boxes.html:
• A set of edges connecting every vertex together, with no cycles, using the smallest possible total weight
  • Build it greedily: repeatedly add the cheapest available edge that connects a new vertex to the tree so far, without creating a loop — continue until every vertex is included

boxes.heading: Shortest path
boxes.html:
• The path between two vertices with the smallest total weight — not necessarily the fewest edges
  • For a small network, systematically list every reasonable route between the two vertices and add up each one's weights, then compare

blocks.label: Don't just grab the smallest number
blocks.html: For a minimum spanning tree, the cheapest edge in the whole network isn't always usable next — it must connect a vertex already in the tree to one that isn't, without forming a cycle. For shortest-path questions, make sure you've checked every plausible route, not just the most obvious-looking one — a path with more edges can still have a smaller total weight.
The vertex/edge language and degree rule introduced here carry straight over into N3's network problems.

revisionQuestions.q: A network has 5 vertices and 7 edges. Calculate the sum of the degrees of all the vertices.
revisionQuestions.a: Sum of degrees = 2 × number of edges = 2 × 7 = 14.

revisionQuestions.q: Team A has 3 members and Team B has 5 members. Each member of Team A must play each member of Team B exactly once. Calculate the total number of games (edges) in the network.
Six friends meet up and each person shakes hands with every other person exactly once. Calculate the total number of handshakes.
revisionQuestions.a: n(n−1)/2 = 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 handshakes.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the rule used to build a minimum spanning tree for a network.
revisionQuestions.a: Starting from any vertex, repeatedly add the cheapest available edge that connects a vertex already in the tree to a vertex not yet included, making sure it doesn't create a cycle. Continue until every vertex is connected — the resulting set of edges is the minimum spanning tree.

revisionQuestions.q: A vertex in a network has degree 5. Explain what this tells you about that vertex.
revisionQuestions.a: The vertex has exactly 5 edges connected to it — meaning it directly connects to 5 other vertices in the network.

revisionQuestions.q: Two vertices, X and Y, are connected by three possible routes with total weights 18, 22 and 15. Determine the shortest path weight between X and Y, and explain your reasoning.
revisionQuestions.a: The shortest path is the route with the smallest total weight, which is 15 — "shortest path" refers to the minimum total weight, not the fewest edges, so the route weighing 15 is the shortest even though it might have more edges than the others.

boxes.heading: Activity networks & the critical path
boxes.html:
• Nodes represent milestones; directed edges (arrows) represent activities/tasks, each with a duration
  • The project's minimum completion time is the length of its longest path from start to finish — this is the critical path
  • To find it: list every path from start to finish, add up each path's durations, and take the longest total

boxes.heading: Float (slack) time
boxes.html:
• An activity not on the critical path has float — spare time it can be delayed without pushing back the whole project
  • Every activity on the critical path has zero float — any delay there delays the entire project

boxes.heading: EST — earliest start time
boxes.html:
• The earliest an activity/node can start, based on the longest path of activities that must finish before it
  • Worked forward from the start of the project

boxes.heading: LST — latest start time
boxes.html:
• The latest an activity/node can start without delaying the whole project's finish
  • Worked backward from the required project finish time
  • A node where EST = LST lies on the critical path — there's no room to delay it

blocks.caption: Critical path analysis at a glance

rows.label: What it means
rows.html: Longest path from start to finish; sets the minimum project duration

rows.label: What it means
rows.html: Spare time an activity can be delayed without affecting the finish — zero on the critical path

rows.label: What it means
rows.html: Earliest an activity/node can start, given everything before it

rows.label: What it means
rows.html: Latest an activity/node can start without delaying the whole project

boxes.heading: Maximum flow & minimum cut
boxes.html:
• The maximum flow is the greatest amount that can travel from a source to a sink, limited by the capacities of the edges (pipes/paths) along each route
  • A cut is a set of edges that, if removed, completely separates the source from the sink — its capacity is the sum of the capacities of the edges it contains

boxes.heading: The max-flow-min-cut theorem
boxes.html:
• The maximum possible flow can never exceed the capacity of any cut — so a cut of capacity 30 means the maximum flow is at most 30 ("30 or less")
  • The true maximum flow equals the smallest (minimum) cut capacity found anywhere in the network

blocks.label: Whole paths and upper bounds, not single numbers
blocks.html: For critical path questions, always total up the whole path, not just one activity's time — the critical path is about which route has the greatest total duration. For flow questions, remember a given cut only sets an upper bound on the max flow (max flow ≤ cut capacity) — never assume the cut shown is automatically the minimum one unless the question confirms it.
This topic builds directly on the vertex/edge language from N2 — Network Concepts, applied to directed, time-weighted (or capacity-weighted) networks.

revisionQuestions.q: A project has two possible paths from start to finish: Path 1 takes 5 + 8 + 3 = 16 days, Path 2 takes 6 + 4 + 9 = 19 days. Determine the minimum time to complete the project and identify the critical path.
revisionQuestions.a: The critical path is the longest path — Path 2, totalling 19 days. The minimum time to complete the whole project is 19 days.

revisionQuestions.q: An activity has an EST of 12 and an LST of 12. Explain what this tells you about that activity.
revisionQuestions.a: Since EST equals LST, the activity has zero float — it must start exactly on time or the whole project will be delayed. This means the activity lies on the critical path.

revisionQuestions.q: An activity is not on the critical path and has a float of 4 days. Explain what this means for scheduling that activity.
revisionQuestions.a: The activity can be delayed by up to 4 days (or take up to 4 days longer than planned) without affecting the overall project completion time, since it has 4 days of spare time before it would start delaying the critical path.

revisionQuestions.q: A cut in a flow network has a total capacity of 45. Explain what the max-flow-min-cut theorem tells you about the maximum possible flow through this network.
revisionQuestions.a: The theorem states the maximum flow can never exceed the capacity of any cut, so the maximum flow through this network is at most 45. The true maximum flow equals the smallest cut capacity found anywhere in the network — 45 is only the actual maximum if no smaller cut exists elsewhere.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the difference between EST and LST for an activity in a project network.
revisionQuestions.a: EST (earliest start time) is the earliest an activity can begin, based on the longest path of activities that must be completed before it. LST (latest start time) is the latest an activity can begin without delaying the whole project's completion, worked backward from the required finish time.

revisionQuestions.q: A project network has four possible start-to-finish paths, of total length 14, 17, 21 and 19 days. State the minimum project completion time and explain your reasoning.
revisionQuestions.a: The minimum completion time is 21 days, since the project cannot finish until every activity — including those on the longest path — is complete. The longest path (21 days) is the critical path and determines the overall minimum duration.

boxes.heading: Sampling methods
boxes.html:
• Random sample — every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen
  • Stratified sample — population split into groups (strata), sample taken from each group proportional to its size: sample from a stratum = (stratum size ÷ population size) × total sample size
  • Self-selected/voluntary response (e.g. an open online survey) — people choose whether to participate, which usually introduces bias since motivated or opinionated people are over-represented

boxes.heading: Types of data
boxes.html:
• Categorical — names/labels (e.g. eye colour) — can't be meaningfully averaged
  • Numerical — discrete: countable whole numbers (e.g. number of siblings)
  • Numerical — continuous: measured, can take any value in a range (e.g. height)

boxes.heading: Measures of centre & spread
boxes.html:
• Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values
  • Median = the middle value of the ordered data (average of the two middle values if there's an even number)
  • Mode = the most frequently occurring value
  • Range = highest − lowest; IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ (spread of the middle 50%, not affected by outliers the way range is)

boxes.heading: Adding a value to a dataset
boxes.html:
• An extreme new value pulls the mean noticeably, since the mean uses every actual value
  • The median shifts only a little (or not at all), since it just depends on position in the ordered list — this is why the median is preferred over the mean for skewed data or data with outliers

rows.label: What it shows
rows.html: Every actual data value, split into stem + leaf

rows.label: Key reading skill
rows.html: Mode = the most-repeated leaf on a stem

rows.label: Key reading skill
rows.html: Skew direction comes from the tail — long tail right = positive skew, long tail left = negative skew

rows.label: What it shows
rows.html: Running total of frequency up to each value

boxes.heading: Outliers — the 1.5×IQR rule
boxes.html:
• A value is an outlier if it falls below Q₁ − 1.5×IQR or above Q₃ + 1.5×IQR
  • Always calculate both boundaries explicitly before deciding — don't just eyeball whether a value "looks far away"

boxes.heading: Skewness — reading the shape
boxes.html:
• Positively skewed (right-skewed): long tail to the right, most data bunched at the lower end — mean > median (the tail pulls the mean up)
  • Negatively skewed (left-skewed): long tail to the left — mean < median

boxes.heading: Finding a required score
boxes.html:
• To find the mark needed on a future test to reach a target overall mean: (current total + needed score) ÷ (total number of tests) = target mean, then solve for the needed score
  • Find the "current total" first by multiplying the current mean by the number of tests so far

boxes.heading: Working backward from a target
boxes.html:
• The same equation can be rearranged the other way — e.g. given the required future score and target mean, you can find what the earlier mean must have been
  • Whichever value is unknown, set up the same total-marks equation and solve for it

blocks.label: Calculate outlier boundaries, don't eyeball them
blocks.html: For 5-number-summary/outlier questions, always work out Q₁ − 1.5×IQR and Q₃ + 1.5×IQR explicitly and compare the data value to those numbers. A value can look "far away" on a small scale without technically being an outlier, or vice versa — the calculation is the only reliable check.

The summary statistics and displays covered here are the foundation for every later statistics topic in the course — comparing datasets, describing distributions, and reading graphs all build on the skills in this topic.

revisionQuestions.q: A school has 1200 students, with 180 in Year 8. A stratified sample of 300 students is to be taken. Calculate how many Year 8 students should be included.
Explain why a voluntary online survey is likely to produce biased results.
revisionQuestions.a: Only people who choose to respond are included, and those with strong opinions or a particular interest in the topic are more likely to participate than a random cross-section of the population. This means the sample isn't representative of everyone, unlike genuine random or stratified sampling.

revisionQuestions.q: A dataset has Q1 = 8, median = 14, Q3 = 20. Determine whether a value of 33 is an outlier, showing your calculation.
revisionQuestions.a: IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ = 20 − 8 = 12. Upper boundary = Q₃ + 1.5×IQR = 20 + 18 = 38. Since 33 < 38, 33 is not an outlier.

revisionQuestions.q: A histogram of a dataset has a long tail extending to the right, with most values bunched toward the lower end. Describe the skew of this distribution and state whether the mean or median would be higher.
revisionQuestions.a: This is positively skewed (right-skewed). The long tail on the right pulls the mean upward more than the median, so the mean is higher than the median.

revisionQuestions.q: After 4 tests, a student has a mean mark of 68. Determine the mark needed on the 5th test to raise the mean to 72.
revisionQuestions.a: Total after 4 tests = 4 × 68 = 272. Needed total after 5 tests = 5 × 72 = 360. Required mark = 360 − 272 = 88.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why the median is less affected than the mean when an extreme value (an outlier) is added to a dataset.
revisionQuestions.a: The mean is calculated using the actual value of every data point, so one very large or small number can pull it substantially. The median only depends on the position of the middle value(s) in the ordered dataset — adding one extreme value shifts that middle position only slightly at most, so the median barely changes.

boxes.heading: Basic probability
boxes.html:
• P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total possible outcomes (for equally likely outcomes) — express as a fraction, decimal or percentage
  • Complementary events: P(not A) = 1 − P(A)

boxes.heading: Two-way tables
boxes.html:
• Organises data by two categories at once (e.g. age group × a yes/no response)
  • To find a probability from a two-way table: identify the correct row/column total as your denominator, and the specific cell as your numerator

boxes.heading: Tree diagrams for multi-stage events
boxes.html:
• Each branch represents one possible outcome at a stage, labelled with its own probability
  • Multiply probabilities along a single path to find that specific sequence's probability
  • Add the probabilities of separate paths that all satisfy the same overall event

boxes.heading: With vs. without replacement
boxes.html:
• With replacement: the selected item is returned before the next draw, so probabilities stay the same at every stage
  • Without replacement: the item isn't returned, so the total (and the count of whichever type was drawn) decreases — the next stage's probabilities change

blocks.caption: Worked example — drawing 2 lollies without replacement (4 mint, 6 vanilla)

rows.label: Step
rows.html: 2. P(second is vanilla | first was mint)

boxes.heading: Relative frequency
boxes.html:
• Relative frequency = number of times an event occurs ÷ total number of trials
  • Used as an estimate of the true probability when it isn't known theoretically (e.g. a possibly biased die) — the more trials carried out, the more reliable the estimate

boxes.heading: Estimating a biased probability
boxes.html:
• If a die is biased so one outcome has a different probability but the rest are all equal to each other, first estimate the biased outcome's probability from its relative frequency
  • The remaining probability (1 − that estimate) is then shared equally among the other equally-likely outcomes

blocks.label: Relabel every stage in a "without replacement" tree
blocks.html: For "without replacement" problems, the total (and possibly the count of one type) changes for every subsequent branch — write out the new fraction at each stage rather than reusing the first stage's numbers. This is the single most common source of errors in multi-stage probability questions.
The sampling-bias questions that reappear here (radio call-ins, pop-up surveys) are the same self-selected sampling concept taught in S1 — Data Analysis — see that topic for the full explanation.

revisionQuestions.q: A bag contains 5 red and 7 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. Calculate the probability it is red, expressed as a fraction.
A box has 3 chocolate and 5 strawberry lollies. Kim selects one and eats it, then Sam selects one from the remaining lollies. Calculate the probability both select a chocolate lolly.
revisionQuestions.a: P(first chocolate) = 3/8. P(second chocolate | first chocolate) = 2/7. P(both chocolate) = 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28.

revisionQuestions.q: A coin is biased so that P(heads) = 0.6. Calculate the probability of getting at least one head in two throws.
revisionQuestions.a: P(no heads) = 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16. P(at least one head) = 1 − 0.16 = 0.84.

revisionQuestions.q: A ten-sided die is biased so that P(rolling a 1) = 0.3, and the remaining 9 outcomes are all equally likely. Calculate the probability of rolling a 7.
revisionQuestions.a: Remaining probability = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7, shared equally among 9 outcomes: 0.7 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.078.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain the difference between "with replacement" and "without replacement" in a two-stage probability experiment.
revisionQuestions.a: With replacement, the selected item is returned before the next draw, so the probabilities are identical at every stage. Without replacement, the item is not returned, so the total number of items (and the count of whichever type was drawn) decreases for the next stage, changing its probabilities.

revisionQuestions.q: A die is rolled 120 times and lands on 6 a total of 15 times. Explain how this result is used to estimate the probability of rolling a 6, and state that estimate.
revisionQuestions.a: The relative frequency (15 ÷ 120 = 0.125) is used as an estimate of the true probability, since the true probability isn't known for a possibly biased die. Estimate: P(6) ≈ 0.125. This estimate becomes more reliable the more trials are carried out.

boxes.heading: Scatterplots & describing association
boxes.html:
• Each point represents one pair of values (x, y)
  • Describe the overall pattern by its form (linear or non-linear), direction (positive — both increase together; negative — one increases as the other decreases), and strength (how closely the points cluster around a line)

boxes.heading: Pearson's correlation coefficient (r)
boxes.html:
• Ranges from −1 to +1 — the sign shows direction, the magnitude (closeness to 1) shows strength
  • r = +1 is a perfect positive linear relationship, r = −1 a perfect negative one, r = 0 means no linear relationship at all

boxes.heading: Least-squares regression line
boxes.html:
• The "line of best fit" — a straight line (y = mx + b) that minimises the overall distance between the points and the line
  • Gives a formula for predicting y from a given x

boxes.heading: Interpreting the equation in context
boxes.html:
• The gradient — how much y changes for each 1-unit increase in x, stated in the actual context's units (e.g. "weight increases by 0.5 kg per extra year of age")
  • The y-intercept — the predicted value of y when x = 0. Check this actually makes sense in context; sometimes x = 0 isn't realistic (e.g. an age of 0)

boxes.heading: Extrapolation vs. interpolation
boxes.html:
• Interpolation — predicting a y value for an x within the range of the original data — generally reliable
  • Extrapolation — predicting outside that range — less reliable, since the linear pattern observed might not continue to hold

boxes.heading: Correlation is not causation
boxes.html:
• A strong correlation between two variables doesn't prove one causes the other
  • There could be a third factor influencing both, or the relationship could simply be coincidental

blocks.label: Interpret in context, in units
blocks.html: When asked to interpret a gradient or intercept from a regression equation, always answer in the actual context's units and describe what a one-unit change in x means for y — don't just restate the numbers from the equation without explaining what they represent.
Bivariate data analysis builds on the single-variable summary statistics and data-display skills from S1 — Data Analysis, extended to look at the relationship between two numerical variables.

revisionQuestions.q: A scatterplot shows a strong upward linear trend between hours of exercise per week and resting heart rate improvement. State the likely sign of the correlation coefficient and describe the strength.
revisionQuestions.a: Since the trend is upward, the correlation is positive; since it's described as strong, |r| would be close to 1 (roughly above 0.7).

revisionQuestions.q: A least-squares regression line is given by y = 12 + 3x, relating x (hours of study) to y (test score). Interpret the value of the gradient (3) in context.
revisionQuestions.a: For each extra hour of study, the test score is predicted to increase by 3 marks, on average.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why extrapolating a regression line beyond the range of the original data can be unreliable.
revisionQuestions.a: The linear pattern observed within the data's range might not continue to hold outside that range — there's no evidence the relationship stays linear (or even exists at all) beyond where data was actually collected, so predictions made there are far less trustworthy.

revisionQuestions.q: Two variables have a correlation coefficient of r = −0.85. Describe the direction and strength of this relationship.
revisionQuestions.a: The negative sign means the direction is negative (as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease). The magnitude, 0.85, indicates a strong relationship.

revisionQuestions.q: Explain why a strong correlation between ice cream sales and shark attacks does not mean one causes the other.
revisionQuestions.a: Both variables are likely influenced by a third factor — warmer weather — which increases both ice cream sales and the number of people swimming in the ocean (and therefore shark encounters). The correlation reflects this shared cause, not a direct causal link between ice cream and shark attacks.

revisionQuestions.q: A regression line is C = 20 + 4n, where C is total cost in dollars and n is the number of items produced. Interpret the y-intercept (20) in this context.
revisionQuestions.a: The y-intercept represents the predicted cost when n = 0 items are produced — i.e. a fixed cost of $20 that applies regardless of how many items are made (e.g. a setup or base cost).

boxes.heading: The normal distribution & the empirical rule
boxes.html:
• A symmetric, bell-shaped curve centred on the mean
  • Empirical (68–95–99.7) rule: about 68% of data lies within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD

boxes.heading: Z-scores
boxes.html:
• z = (x − mean) ÷ SD — measures how many standard deviations a value x is from the mean
  • z = 0 is exactly at the mean; positive z is above the mean, negative z is below it

boxes.heading: Comparing values from different distributions
boxes.html:
• To compare performance across tests/populations with different means and SDs, convert each value to a z-score first
  • The higher z-score is relatively better — even if its actual/raw value is lower than the other

boxes.heading: Finding an actual value from a z-score
boxes.html:
• Rearrange the z-score formula: x = mean + z × SD
  • Substitute the known mean, SD and z-score to find the actual data value

blocks.caption: The empirical rule at a glance

boxes.heading: Using standard normal (Z) tables
boxes.html:
• Exam tables usually give P(Z < z) or P(0 < Z < z) for positive z
  • Key symmetry facts: P(Z < 0) = 0.5 (half the data is below the mean); P(0 < Z < z) = P(Z < z) − 0.5; P(Z > z) = 1 − P(Z < z)
  • For negative z, use symmetry: P(Z < −z) = P(Z > z) — the same distance below the mean mirrors above it

boxes.heading: Recognising a normal distribution from a histogram
boxes.html:
• Roughly symmetric, bell-shaped, with a single central peak (unimodal)
  • Tapering tails on both sides
  • A clearly skewed or multi-peaked histogram is not normal

blocks.label: Sketch the bell curve first
blocks.html: Before using a table or the empirical rule, sketch the bell curve and shade the exact region the question is asking about. This avoids the classic mistake of forgetting to add or subtract 0.5 when converting between a "less than the mean" table value and a one-sided region.
Recognising a normal shape here connects back to S1 — Data Analysis's work on histograms and skew — a normal distribution is simply the special case with zero skew.

revisionQuestions.q: Test scores are normally distributed with mean 65 and standard deviation 8. Calculate the z-score for a mark of 81.
A distribution has mean 40 and standard deviation 6. Calculate the actual value corresponding to a z-score of −1.5.
Using the empirical rule, estimate the percentage of data that lies between the mean and 2 standard deviations above the mean.
revisionQuestions.a: 95% lies within 2 SD of the mean (both sides combined), so exactly half of that — 47.5% — lies between the mean and 2 SD above it.

revisionQuestions.q: A student scored a z-score of 1.6 in English and 2.1 in Maths, relative to their respective class distributions. Explain which subject the student performed better in relative to their class.
revisionQuestions.a: The higher z-score (2.1 in Maths) means the student performed further above their class's mean, in terms of standard deviations, than in English (1.6) — so relatively, the student did better in Maths, even without knowing the actual raw marks.

revisionQuestions.q: A standard normal table gives P(Z < 1.2) = 0.8849. Calculate P(0 < Z < 1.2).
Explain two features of a histogram that would suggest the underlying data is normally distributed.
revisionQuestions.a: (1) The histogram is roughly symmetric about a central value. (2) It has a single peak (unimodal), with the bars tapering off gradually on both sides, rather than being skewed or having multiple separate peaks.
